title: 2 Kings

stories.title: 🔥 2 Kings 1
summaryBullets: After the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against Israel. (1:1).

Now Ahaziah had fallen through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria and injured himself. So he sent messengers and instructed them: “Go inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover from this injury.” (1:2).

But the angel of the LORD said to Elijah the Tishbite, “Go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria and ask them, ‘Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are on your way to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?’ (1:3).
Therefore this is what the LORD says: ‘You will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.’” So Elijah departed. (1:4).
When the messengers returned to the king, he asked them, “Why have you returned?” (1:5).

They replied, “A man came up to meet us and said, ‘Go back to the king who sent you and tell him that this is what the LORD says: Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are sending these men to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.’” (1:6).
The king asked them, “What sort of man came up to meet you and spoke these words to you?” (1:7).
“He was a hairy man,” they answered, “with a leather belt around his waist.” “It was Elijah the Tishbite,” said the king. (1:8).

Then King Ahaziah sent to Elijah a captain with his company of fifty men. So the captain went up to Elijah, who was sitting on top of a hill, and said to him, “Man of God, the king declares, ‘Come down!’” (1:9).

Elijah answered the captain, “If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.” And fire came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men. (1:10).
So the king sent to Elijah another captain with his fifty men. And the captain said to Elijah, “Man of God, the king declares, ‘Come down at once!’” (1:11).

Again Elijah replied, “If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.” And the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men. (1:12).

So the king sent a third captain with his fifty men. And the third captain went up, fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged him, “Man of God, may my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours please be precious in your sight. (1:13).
Behold, fire has come down from heaven and consumed the first two captains of fifty, with all their men. But now may my life be precious in your sight.” (1:14).
Then the angel of the LORD said to Elijah, “Go down with him. Do not be afraid of him.” So Elijah got up and went down with him to the king. (1:15).

And Elijah said to King Ahaziah, “This is what the LORD says: Is there really no God in Israel for you to inquire of His word? Is that why you have sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.” (1:16).

So Ahaziah died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken. And since he had no son, Jehoram succeeded him in the second year of the reign of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat over Judah. (1:17).
As for the rest of the acts of Ahaziah, along with his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? (1:18).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 22:51-53: Ahaziah reigns two years, serves Baal, and provokes the LORD exactly as his father did.
Deuteronomy 18:10-12: No one among you shall practise divination or inquire of the dead; all who do these things are detestable to the LORD.
Luke 9:51-56: James and John ask whether to call fire down from heaven on a village, and Jesus turns and rebukes them.
1 Kings 18:36-38: Fire falls from heaven at Carmel and consumes the offering, the wood, the stones, the dust, and the water.
Matthew 12:24-27: The Pharisees say Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּעַל זְבוּב (Baal zevuv), lord of flies
translationNotes.note: The god Ahaziah sends to consult in verse 2. Baal was the Canaanite storm god, and this local title reads as lord of the flies, which in a hot country with open sacrifice is a claim to control disease and the swarms that carry it. Sending to a Philistine shrine for a medical verdict is the point of the rebuke in verse 3. The Greek form of the name, Beelzeboul, is used of the prince of demons in Matthew 12:24.

The northernmost of the five Philistine cities, about thirty miles west of Jerusalem on the edge of the coastal plain. Ahaziah sends messengers past every shrine in his own kingdom to ask a Philistine god about his injury. A dedicatory inscription naming Ekron and its rulers was found at the site in 1996, confirming the identification.

translationNotes.term: The upper room and its lattice
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲלִיָּה (aliyah), roof chamber - שְׂבָכָה (sevakhah), lattice
translationNotes.note: Verse 2 has the king fall through the lattice of his upper room. A house of any standing carried a room built on the flat roof, cooler than the rooms below and used for sleeping and for guests; the prophet's room at 1 Kings 17:19 and Elisha's at 2 Kings 4:10 are the same thing. The opening was closed with a wooden screen rather than glass, and it gave way.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂר חֲמִשִּׁים (sar hamishim), officer of fifty
translationNotes.note: The units sent in verses 9 to 13 are not an arbitrary number of men. Israel's army was organised in thousands, hundreds, and fifties, each with its own commander, the structure Jethro proposes at Exodus 18:21 and Moses adopts at Deuteronomy 1:15. A captain of fifty is a junior officer, and Isaiah 3:3 lists the rank among the props of the state that God removes.

translationNotes.term: A hairy man with a leather belt
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּעַל שֵׂעָר (baal sear), owner of hair
translationNotes.note: Verse 8 identifies Elijah by his appearance alone: a hairy man wearing a leather belt at his waist. That is a description of dress and grooming, not of a wild man, and it marked him out against court officials in linen and dyed wool. Mark 1:6 describes John the Baptist in the same two terms, camel hair with a leather belt around his waist.

stories.keyTakeaway: King Ahaziah, injured from a fall, sends messengers to consult Baal-Zebub; Elijah intercepts them with word from God that Ahaziah will die. After two military captains and their men are consumed by fire from heaven, a third captain approaches humbly and Elijah goes to the king, who dies as prophesied; Joram succeeds him.

stories.title: 🔥 2 Kings 2
summaryBullets: Shortly before the LORD took Elijah up to heaven in a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha were on their way from Gilgal, (2:1).

and Elijah said to Elisha, “Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me on to Bethel.” But Elisha replied, “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” So they went down to Bethel. (2:2).
Then the sons of the prophets at Bethel came out to Elisha and said, “Do you know that the LORD will take your master away from you today?” “Yes, I know,” he replied. “Do not speak of it.” (2:3).

And Elijah said to Elisha, “Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me on to Jericho.” But Elisha replied, “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” So they went to Jericho. (2:4).
Then the sons of the prophets at Jericho came up to Elisha and said, “Do you know that the LORD will take your master away from you today?” “Yes, I know,” he replied. “Do not speak of it.” (2:5).

And Elijah said to Elisha, “Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me on to the Jordan.” But Elisha replied, “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” So the two of them went on. (2:6).
Then a company of fifty of the sons of the prophets went and stood at a distance, facing Elijah and Elisha as the two of them stood by the Jordan. (2:7).
And Elijah took his cloak, rolled it up, and struck the waters, which parted to the right and to the left, so that the two of them crossed over on dry ground. (2:8).
After they had crossed over, Elijah said to Elisha, “Tell me, what can I do for you before I am taken away from you?” “Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit,” Elisha replied. (2:9).
“You have requested a difficult thing,” said Elijah. “Nevertheless, if you see me as I am taken from you, it will be yours. But if not, then it will not be so.” (2:10).
As they were walking along and talking together, suddenly a chariot of fire with horses of fire appeared and separated the two of them, and Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind. (2:11).
As Elisha watched, he cried out, “My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!” And he saw Elijah no more. So taking hold of his own clothes, he tore them in two. (2:12).
Elisha also picked up the cloak that had fallen from Elijah, and he went back and stood on the bank of the Jordan. (2:13).

Then he took the cloak of Elijah that had fallen from him and struck the waters. “Where now is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” he asked. And when he had struck the waters, they parted to the right and to the left, and Elisha crossed over. (2:14).

When the sons of the prophets who were watching him from Jericho saw what had happened, they said, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.” And they went to meet him and bowed down to the ground before him. (2:15).

“Look now,” they said to Elisha, “we your servants have fifty valiant men. Please let them go and search for your master. Perhaps the Spirit of the LORD has taken him up and put him on one of the mountains or in one of the valleys.” “Do not send them,” Elisha replied. (2:16).
But when they pressed him to the point of embarrassment, he said, “Send them.” And they sent fifty men, who searched for three days but did not find Elijah. (2:17).
When they returned to Elisha, who was staying in Jericho, he said to them, “Didn’t I tell you not to go?” (2:18).
Then the men of the city said to Elisha, “Please note, our lord, that the city’s location is good, as you can see. But the water is bad and the land is unfruitful.” (2:19).
“Bring me a new bowl,” he replied, “and put some salt in it.” So they brought it to him, (2:20).
and Elisha went out to the spring, cast the salt into it, and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘I have healed this water. No longer will it cause death or unfruitfulness.’” (2:21).
And the waters there have been healthy to this day, according to the word spoken by Elisha. (2:22).
From there, Elisha went up to Bethel, and as he was walking up the road, a group of boys came out of the city and jeered at him, chanting, “Go up, you baldhead! Go up, you baldhead!” (2:23).
Then he turned around, looked at them, and called down a curse on them in the name of the LORD. Suddenly two female bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of the boys. (2:24).
And Elisha went on to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria. (2:25).
crossRefs: Genesis 5:24: Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him, the only other man Scripture reports as taken without dying.
1 Kings 12:28-30: Jeroboam sets up a golden calf at Bethel and another at Dan and calls them the gods who brought Israel out of Egypt; Bethel is the town the crowd in 2:23 comes out of.
Malachi 4:5-6: I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes.
Joshua 3:14-17: The waters of the Jordan are cut off and Israel crosses over on dry ground, the same river parted twice in this chapter.
Luke 9:28-31: Moses and Elijah appear in glory with Jesus and speak of the departure He was to accomplish at Jerusalem.

translationNotes.note: A heavy outer cloak, the garment a man slept under and could not be kept from him overnight if taken in pledge (Exodus 22:26-27). Elijah's is the object he throws over Elisha to call him from the plough (1 Kings 19:19), rolls up to strike the Jordan in verse 8, and leaves behind in verse 13. Picking it up is the visible transfer of the office.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פִּי שְׁנַיִם (pi shenayim), a mouth of two
translationNotes.note: Elisha's request in verse 9 uses a legal term. The double portion is the firstborn's share of an estate, two parts where every other son gets one, guaranteed at Deuteronomy 21:17 even when the father prefers another son. He is not asking for twice Elijah's spirit; he is asking to be treated as the heir of the man's office.

Companies of prophets living together at Bethel, Jericho, and Gilgal, appearing throughout this chapter and again at 4:38 and 6:1-2. Son of in Hebrew often marks membership in a class rather than descent, so the phrase names a guild under a master. Fifty of them stand off at a distance at the Jordan in verse 7, and one of them is sent to anoint Jehu in chapter 9.

The Hebrew word naar covers anyone from a young child to a man of military age; Joseph is called a naar at seventeen and Solomon uses it of himself as king. Forty-two of them come out of Bethel, the town holding one of Jeroboam's calves, to jeer the prophet out of their territory. The number and the place mark this as a mob, not a handful of children.

The Syrian brown bear lived in the wooded hills of Israel and the Lebanon range into modern times, standing over five feet and weighing several hundred pounds. Scripture treats it as a known danger alongside the lion: David killed both (1 Samuel 17:34-36), and Amos 5:19 pictures a man escaping a lion only to meet a bear.

stories.keyTakeaway: Elijah is taken up to heaven in a chariot of fire after crossing the Jordan; Elisha inherits his cloak and spirit, heals bad water in Jericho with salt, and curses youths who mock him, resulting in bears mauling forty-two of them.

headings.text: Elisha Heals the Waters of Jericho

stories.title: 💧 2 Kings 3
summaryBullets: In the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat’s reign over Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria twelve years. (3:1).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, but not as his father and mother had done. He removed the sacred pillar of Baal that his father had made. (3:2).
Nevertheless, he clung to the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit; he did not turn away from them. (3:3).
Now Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder, and he would render to the king of Israel a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams. (3:4).
But after the death of Ahab, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel. (3:5).
So at that time King Jehoram set out from Samaria and mobilized all Israel. (3:6).

And he sent a message to Jehoshaphat king of Judah: “The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you go with me to fight against Moab?” “I will go,” replied Jehoshaphat. “I am as you are, my people are your people, and my horses are your horses.” (3:7).
Then he asked, “Which way shall we go up?” “By way of the Desert of Edom,” replied Joram. (3:8).
So the king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom set out, and after they had traveled a roundabout route for seven days, they had no water for their army or for their animals. (3:9).
“Alas,” said the king of Israel, “for the LORD has summoned these three kings to deliver them into the hand of Moab!” (3:10).

But Jehoshaphat asked, “Is there no prophet of the LORD here? Let us inquire of the LORD through him.” And one of the servants of the king of Israel answered, “Elisha son of Shaphat is here. He used to pour water on the hands of Elijah.” (3:11).
Jehoshaphat affirmed, “The word of the LORD is with him.” So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom went down to him. (3:12).

Elisha, however, said to the king of Israel, “What have we to do with each other? Go to the prophets of your father and of your mother!” “No,” replied the king of Israel, “for it is the LORD who has summoned these three kings to deliver them into the hand of Moab.” (3:13).

Then Elisha said, “As surely as the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand, were it not for my regard for the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not look at you or acknowledge you. (3:14).
But now, bring me a harpist.” And while the harpist played, the hand of the LORD came upon Elisha (3:15).
and he said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Dig this valley full of ditches.’ (3:16).
For the LORD says, ‘You will not see wind or rain, but the valley will be filled with water, and you will drink— you and your cattle and your animals.’ (3:17).
This is a simple matter in the sight of the LORD, and He will also deliver the Moabites into your hand. (3:18).
And you shall attack every fortified city and every city of importance. You shall cut down every good tree, stop up every spring, and ruin every good field with stones.” (3:19).
The next morning, at the time of the morning sacrifice, water suddenly flowed from the direction of Edom and filled the land. (3:20).
Now all the Moabites had heard that the kings had come up to fight against them. So all who could bear arms, young and old, were summoned and stationed at the border. (3:21).
When they got up early in the morning, the sun was shining on the water, and it looked as red as blood to the Moabites across the way. (3:22).
“This is blood!” they exclaimed. “The kings have clashed swords and slaughtered one another. Now to the plunder, Moab!” (3:23).
But when the Moabites came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose up and attacked them, and they fled before them. So the Israelites invaded their land and struck down the Moabites. (3:24).

They destroyed the cities, and each man threw stones on every good field until it was covered. They stopped up every spring and cut down every good tree. Only Kir-haraseth was left with stones in place, but men with slings surrounded it and attacked it as well. (3:25).
When the king of Moab saw that the battle was too fierce for him, he took with him seven hundred swordsmen to break through to the king of Edom, but they could not prevail. (3:26).

So he took his firstborn son, who was to succeed him, and offered him as a burnt offering on the city wall. And there was great fury against the Israelites, so they withdrew and returned to their own land. (3:27).
crossRefs: Numbers 22:1-6: Balak king of Moab is in dread of Israel and sends for Balaam to curse them.
2 Samuel 8:2: David defeats Moab, measures them with a line, and they become his servants and bring tribute.
Deuteronomy 20:19-20: When you besiege a city a long time, do not destroy its fruit trees by putting an axe to them.
Leviticus 18:21: You shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech, and so profane the name of your God.
1 Kings 22:47-48: There was no king in Edom, only a deputy, and Jehoshaphat's ships were wrecked before they sailed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶבֶד (ʿeved), Greek: δοῦλος (doulos), Aramaic: עבדא (ʿavda)
translationNotes.note: Children could be seized as slaves to pay debts. The oil miracle prevented this fate.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צָרַעַת (ṣaraʿat), Greek: λέπρα (lepra), Aramaic: גרבתא (garbata)
translationNotes.note: Not modern Hansen’s disease but a range of skin conditions causing ritual uncleanness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יַרְדֵּן (Yarden), Greek: Ἰορδάνης (Iordanēs), Aramaic: ירדנא (Yardena)
translationNotes.note: River of Israel central to baptismal symbolism and repeated miracles.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

Chemosh was the national god of Moab; Numbers 21:29 calls the Moabites the people of Chemosh, and Solomon built him a high place east of Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7). Verse 27 reports Mesha taking his oldest son, the heir to his throne, and burning him as an offering on the city wall in full view of the besieging armies. This was what Moab did when a siege went badly, and the text states it without comment.

Mesha left his own account of this war. A black basalt stone found at Dhiban in Jordan in 1868, now in the Louvre, carries thirty-four lines in Moabite in which King Mesha names Omri king of Israel, describes throwing off Israel's rule, and credits Chemosh with the victory. It is the same conflict this chapter reports, told from the other side.

Verse 4 sets Moab's annual tribute at 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams. Moab's plateau east of the Dead Sea is high, dry grazing country, so the payment came in what the land produced. Withholding tribute was how a vassal declared independence, which is what verse 5 records him doing the moment Ahab died.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joram of Israel, with Judah and Edom's help, campaigns against rebellious Moab; Elisha promises water and victory, the armies prevail, and the Moabites are defeated and their land ravaged.

stories.title: 💧 2 Kings 4
summaryBullets: Now the wife of one of the sons of the prophets cried out to Elisha, “Your servant, my husband, is dead, and you know that your servant feared the LORD. And now his creditor is coming to take my two children as his slaves!” (4:1).
“How can I help you?” asked Elisha. “Tell me, what do you have in the house?” She answered, “Your servant has nothing in the house but a jar of oil.” (4:2).
“Go,” said Elisha, “borrow empty jars from all your neighbors. Do not gather just a few. (4:3).
Then go inside, shut the door behind you and your sons, and pour oil into all these jars, setting the full ones aside.” (4:4).
So she left him, and after she had shut the door behind her and her sons, they kept bringing jars to her, and she kept pouring. (4:5).
When all the jars were full, she said to her son, “Bring me another.” But he replied, “There are no more jars.” Then the oil stopped flowing. (4:6).
She went and told the man of God, and he said, “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt. Then you and your sons can live on the remainder.” (4:7).
One day Elisha went to Shunem, and a prominent woman who lived there persuaded him to have a meal. So whenever he would pass by, he would stop there to eat. (4:8).
Then the woman said to her husband, “Behold, now I know that the one who often comes our way is a holy man of God. (4:9).
Please let us make a small room upstairs and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp for him. Then when he comes to us, he can stay there.” (4:10).
One day Elisha came to visit and went to his upper room to lie down. (4:11).
And he said to Gehazi his servant, “Call the Shunammite woman.” And when he had called her, she stood before him, (4:12).

and Elisha said to Gehazi, “Now tell her, ‘Look, you have gone to all this trouble for us. What can we do for you? Can we speak on your behalf to the king or the commander of the army?’” “I have a home among my own people,” she replied. (4:13).
So he asked, “Then what should be done for her?” “Well, she has no son,” Gehazi replied, “and her husband is old.” (4:14).
“Call her,” said Elisha. So Gehazi called her, and she stood in the doorway. (4:15).
And Elisha declared, “At this time next year, you will hold a son in your arms.” “No, my lord,” she said. “Do not lie to your maidservant, O man of God.” (4:16).
But the woman did conceive, and at that time the next year she gave birth to a son, just as Elisha had told her. (4:17).
And the child grew, and one day he went out to his father, who was with the harvesters. (4:18).
“My head! My head!” he complained to his father. So his father told a servant, “Carry him to his mother.” (4:19).
After the servant had picked him up and carried him to his mother, the boy sat on her lap until noon, and then he died. (4:20).
And she went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God. Then she shut the door and went out. (4:21).
And the woman called her husband and said, “Please send me one of the servants and one of the donkeys, that I may go quickly to the man of God and return.” (4:22).
“Why would you go to him today?” he replied. “It is not a New Moon or a Sabbath.” “Everything is all right,” she said. (4:23).
Then she saddled the donkey and told her servant, “Drive onward; do not slow the pace for me unless I tell you.” (4:24).
So she set out and went to the man of God at Mount Carmel. When the man of God saw her at a distance, he said to his servant Gehazi, “Look, there is the Shunammite woman. (4:25).
Please run out now to meet her and ask, ‘Are you all right? Is your husband all right? Is your child all right?’” And she answered, “Everything is all right.” (4:26).

When she reached the man of God at the mountain, she clung to his feet. Gehazi came over to push her away, but the man of God said, “Leave her alone, for her soul is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” (4:27).
Then she said, “Did I ask you for a son, my lord? Didn’t I say, ‘Do not deceive me?’” (4:28).

So Elisha said to Gehazi, “Tie up your garment, take my staff in your hand, and go! If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not answer him. Then lay my staff on the boy’s face.” (4:29).
And the mother of the boy said, “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” So he got up and followed her. (4:30).
Gehazi went on ahead of them and laid the staff on the boy’s face, but there was no sound or response. So he went back to meet Elisha and told him, “The boy has not awakened.” (4:31).
When Elisha reached the house, there was the boy lying dead on his bed. (4:32).
So he went in, closed the door behind the two of them, and prayed to the LORD. (4:33).
Then Elisha got on the bed and lay on the boy, mouth to mouth, eye to eye, and hand to hand. As he stretched himself out over him, the boy’s body became warm. (4:34).
Elisha turned away and paced back and forth across the room. Then he got on the bed and stretched himself out over the boy again, and the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes. (4:35).
Elisha summoned Gehazi and said, “Call the Shunammite woman.” So he called her and she came. Then Elisha said, “Pick up your son.” (4:36).
She came in, fell at his feet, and bowed to the ground. Then she picked up her son and went out. (4:37).

When Elisha returned to Gilgal, there was a famine in the land. As the sons of the prophets were sitting at his feet, he said to his attendant, “Put on the large pot and boil some stew for the sons of the prophets.” (4:38).

One of them went out to the field to gather herbs, and he found a wild vine from which he gathered as many wild gourds as his garment could hold. Then he came back and cut them up into the pot of stew, though no one knew what they were. (4:39).
And they poured it out for the men to eat, but when they tasted the stew they cried out, “There is death in the pot, O man of God!” And they could not eat it. (4:40).
Then Elisha said, “Get some flour.” He threw it into the pot and said, “Pour it out for the people to eat.” And there was nothing harmful in the pot. (4:41).
Now a man from Baal-shalishah came to the man of God with a sack of twenty loaves of barley bread from the first ripe grain. “Give it to the people to eat,” said Elisha. (4:42).

But his servant asked, “How am I to set twenty loaves before a hundred men?” “Give it to the people to eat,” said Elisha, “for this is what the LORD says: ‘They will eat and have some left over.’” (4:43).
So he set it before them, and they ate and had some left over, according to the word of the LORD. (4:44).
crossRefs: Exodus 21:2-7: A Hebrew bought as a slave serves six years and goes out free in the seventh, owing nothing.
Leviticus 25:39-43: A poor Israelite who sells himself is not to be treated as a slave but as a hired worker, until the Jubilee.
1 Kings 17:8-24: Elijah, the widow of Zarephath, the jar of flour that did not run out, and her son restored to life.
Matthew 14:15-21: Five loaves and two fish feed five thousand men, and twelve baskets of pieces are gathered up.
John 6:9-13: A boy has five barley loaves and two fish, and after all have eaten their fill twelve baskets remain.

stories.title: 💧 2 Kings 5
summaryBullets: Now Naaman, the commander of the army of the king of Aram, was a great man in his master’s sight and highly regarded, for through him the LORD had given victory to Aram. And he was a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. (5:1).
At this time the Arameans had gone out in bands and had taken a young girl from the land of Israel, and she was serving Naaman’s wife. (5:2).
She said to her mistress, “If only my master would go to the prophet who is in Samaria, he would cure him of his leprosy.” (5:3).
And Naaman went and told his master what the girl from the land of Israel had said. (5:4).

“Go now,” said the king of Aram, “and I will send you with a letter to the king of Israel.” So Naaman departed, taking with him ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, and ten sets of clothing. (5:5).
And the letter that he took to the king of Israel stated: “With this letter I am sending my servant Naaman, so that you may cure him of his leprosy.” (5:6).

When the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and asked, “Am I God, killing and giving life, that this man expects me to cure a leper? Surely you can see that he is seeking a quarrel with me!” (5:7).

Now when Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, he sent a message to the king: “Why have you torn your clothes? Please let the man come to me, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel.” (5:8).
So Naaman came with his horses and chariots and stood at the door of Elisha’s house. (5:9).
Then Elisha sent him a messenger, who said, “Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean.” (5:10).
But Naaman went away angry, saying, “I thought that he would surely come out, stand and call on the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the spot to cure my leprosy. (5:11).
Are not the Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Could I not have washed in them and been cleansed?” So he turned and went away in a rage. (5:12).

Naaman’s servants, however, approached him and said, “My father, if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, would you not have done it? How much more, then, when he tells you, ‘Wash and be cleansed’?” (5:13).
So Naaman went down and dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored and became like that of a little child, and he was clean. (5:14).

Then Naaman and all his attendants went back to the man of God, stood before him, and declared, “Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. So please accept a gift from your servant.” (5:15).
But Elisha replied, “As surely as the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it.” And although Naaman urged him to accept it, he refused. (5:16).

“If you will not,” said Naaman, “please let me, your servant, be given as much soil as a pair of mules can carry. For your servant will never again make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to any other god but the LORD. (5:17).

Yet may the LORD forgive your servant this one thing: When my master goes into the temple of Rimmon to worship there, and he leans on my arm, and I bow down in the temple of Rimmon, may the LORD forgive your servant in this matter.” (5:18).
“Go in peace,” said Elisha. But after Naaman had traveled a short distance, (5:19).

Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, “Look, my master has spared this Aramean, Naaman, by not accepting what he brought. As surely as the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him.” (5:20).
So Gehazi pursued Naaman. And when Naaman saw him running toward him, he got down from the chariot to meet him and asked, “Is everything all right?” (5:21).

“Everything is all right,” Gehazi replied. “My master has sent me to say, ‘Look, two young men from the sons of the prophets have just now come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them a talent of silver and two sets of clothing.’” (5:22).

But Naaman insisted, “Please, take two talents.” And he urged Gehazi to accept them. Then he tied up two talents of silver in two bags along with two sets of clothing and gave them to two of his servants, who carried them ahead of Gehazi. (5:23).
When Gehazi came to the hill, he took the gifts from the servants and stored them in the house. Then he dismissed the men, and they departed. (5:24).
When Gehazi went in and stood before his master, Elisha asked him, “Gehazi, where have you been?” “Your servant did not go anywhere,” he replied. (5:25).

But Elisha questioned him, “Did not my spirit go with you when the man got down from his chariot to meet you? Is this the time to accept money and clothing, olive groves and vineyards, sheep and oxen, menservants and maidservants? (5:26).
Therefore, the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and your descendants forever!” And as Gehazi left his presence, he was leprous— as white as snow. (5:27).

The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

About 75 lbs (34 kg) of metal. A 'talent of gold' in the Old Testament (e.g. 2 Samuel 12:30) refers to physical mass rather than coined currency. The bronze for the Tabernacle (Exodus 38:29) was 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

Naaman asks in verse 17 to carry Israelite soil home to Damascus. Ancient religion generally tied a god to his territory, so a foreigner who wanted to sacrifice to the God of Israel took ground from Israel to build his altar on. The request shows what he had grasped and what he had not, and the text records it without correcting him.

The temple in Damascus in verse 18 belonged to the Aramean storm god Hadad, called Rammanu, the thunderer, in Akkadian, which is where the name Rimmon comes from. Zechariah 12:11 preserves the fuller form Hadad-rimmon. As the king's chief officer, Naaman had to attend the king in that temple and support him when he bowed.

translationNotes.term: Ten talents and six thousand shekels
translationNotes.note: Verse 5 has Naaman set out with ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, and ten changes of clothing. A talent is about 75 pounds, so that is roughly 750 pounds of silver and, at about 0.4 ounces to the shekel, some 150 pounds of gold. It is a king's ransom for a cure, and Elisha will not take any of it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Naaman, an Aramean military commander with leprosy, travels to Israel on his king's behalf; after initially resisting Elisha's instruction to wash in the Jordan, he obeys and is healed, then offers gifts that Elisha refuses. Elisha's servant Gehazi lies to obtain silver and clothing from Naaman, and Elisha strikes him with Naaman's leprosy as punishment.

stories.title: 💧 2 Kings 6
summaryBullets: Now the sons of the prophets said to Elisha, “Please take note that the place where we meet with you is too small for us. (6:1).
Please let us go to the Jordan, where each of us can get a log so we can build ourselves a place to live there.” “Go,” said Elisha. (6:2).
Then one of them said, “Please come with your servants.” “I will come,” he replied. (6:3).
So Elisha went with them, and when they came to the Jordan, they began to cut down some trees. (6:4).
As one of them was cutting down a tree, the iron axe head fell into the water. “Oh, my master,” he cried out, “it was borrowed!” (6:5).
“Where did it fall?” asked the man of God. And when he showed him the place, the man of God cut a stick, threw it there, and made the iron float. (6:6).
“Lift it out,” he said, and the man reached out his hand and took it. (6:7).
Now the king of Aram was at war against Israel. After consulting with his servants, he said, “My camp will be in such and such a place.” (6:8).
Then the man of God sent word to the king of Israel: “Be careful not to pass by this place, for the Arameans are going down there.” (6:9).
So the king of Israel sent word to the place the man of God had pointed out. Time and again Elisha warned the king, so that he was on his guard in such places. (6:10).
For this reason the king of Aram became enraged and called his servants to demand of them, “Tell me, which one of us is on the side of the king of Israel?” (6:11).
But one of his servants replied, “No one, my lord the king. For Elisha, the prophet in Israel, tells the king of Israel the very words you speak in your bedroom.” (6:12).
So the king said, “Go and see where he is, that I may send men to capture him.” On receiving the report, “Elisha is in Dothan,” (6:13).
the king of Aram sent horses, chariots, and a great army. They went there by night and surrounded the city. (6:14).

When the servant of the man of God got up and went out early in the morning, behold, an army with horses and chariots had surrounded the city. So he asked Elisha, “Oh, my master, what are we to do?” (6:15).
“Do not be afraid,” Elisha answered, “for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” (6:16).

Then Elisha prayed, “O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see.” And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw that the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha. (6:17).
As the Arameans came down against him, Elisha prayed to the LORD, “Please strike these people with blindness.” So He struck them with blindness, according to the word of Elisha. (6:18).
And Elisha told them, “This is not the way, and this is not the city. Follow me, and I will take you to the man you are seeking.” And he led them to Samaria. (6:19).

When they had entered Samaria, Elisha said, “O LORD, open the eyes of these men that they may see.” Then the LORD opened their eyes, and they looked around and discovered that they were in Samaria. (6:20).
And when the king of Israel saw them, he asked Elisha, “My father, shall I kill them? Shall I kill them?” (6:21).

“Do not kill them,” he replied. “Would you kill those you have captured with your own sword or bow? Set food and water before them, that they may eat and drink and then return to their master.” (6:22).

So the king prepared a great feast for them, and after they had finished eating and drinking, he sent them away, and they returned to their master. And the Aramean raiders did not come into the land of Israel again. (6:23).
Some time later, Ben-hadad king of Aram assembled his entire army and marched up to besiege Samaria. (6:24).

So there was a great famine in Samaria. Indeed, they besieged the city so long that a donkey’s head sold for eighty shekels of silver, and a quarter cab of dove’s dung sold for five shekels of silver. (6:25).
As the king of Israel was passing by on the wall, a woman cried out to him, “Help me, my lord the king!” (6:26).
He answered, “If the LORD does not help you, where can I find help for you? From the threshing floor or the winepress?” (6:27).
Then the king asked her, “What is the matter?” And she answered, “This woman said to me, ‘Give up your son, that we may eat him, and tomorrow we will eat my son.’ (6:28).
So we boiled my son and ate him, and the next day I said to her, ‘Give up your son, that we may eat him.’ But she had hidden her son.” (6:29).
When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes. And as he passed by on the wall, the people saw the sackcloth under his clothes next to his skin. (6:30).
He announced, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if the head of Elisha son of Shaphat remains on his shoulders through this day!” (6:31).

Now Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. The king sent a messenger ahead, but before he arrived, Elisha said to the elders, “Do you see how this murderer has sent someone to cut off my head? Look, when the messenger comes, shut the door to keep him out. Is not the sound of his master’s footsteps behind him?” (6:32).
While Elisha was still speaking with them, the messenger came down to him. And the king said, “This calamity is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?” (6:33).

Leviticus 26:27-29: If you still walk contrary to Me, you will eat the flesh of your sons and the flesh of your daughters.
Numbers 22:31: The LORD opens Balaam's eyes and he sees the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword.

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Verse 25 records a donkey's head selling for eighty shekels of silver and a quarter of a kab of dove's dung for five. A donkey is unclean and the head is the least edible part of it; a quarter kab is roughly half a pint. A shekel is about 0.4 ounces of silver, and Exodus 21:32 values a slave's life at thirty shekels, so the head of an unclean animal was going for nearly three times the price of a person. The next chapter has fine flour back at a shekel a seah (2 Kings 7:1).

An army rarely stormed a walled city. It surrounded it, cut the roads, camped, and waited for the food to run out, which could take months or years; Samaria itself later held out three years (2 Kings 17:5). The people inside had grain pits and cisterns and nothing else, and the horrors listed in Deuteronomy 28:53-57 as covenant curses are a straight description of what happened when those ran dry.

stories.keyTakeaway: The prophets expand their meeting place by the Jordan, and Elisha miraculously recovers a borrowed axhead from the water; later, when the king of Aram besieges Samaria, Elisha blinds the Aramean army, leads them to the city, and the king feeds them instead of killing them, stopping the raids. When Ben-Hadad later lays siege to Samaria causing famine and cannibalism within the city, the desperate king blames Elisha and sends someone to kill him, but Elisha tells the elders the king's murderous messenger is coming.

headings.text: The Siege and Famine of Samaria

stories.title: 💧 2 Kings 7
summaryBullets: Then Elisha said, “Hear the word of the LORD! This is what the LORD says: ‘About this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria, a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel, and two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel.’” (7:1).

But the officer on whose arm the king leaned answered the man of God, “Look, even if the LORD were to make windows in heaven, could this really happen?” “You will see it with your own eyes,” replied Elisha, “but you will not eat any of it.” (7:2).
Now there were four men with leprosy at the entrance of the city gate, and they said to one another, “Why just sit here until we die? (7:3).

If we say, ‘Let us go into the city,’ we will die there from the famine in the city; but if we sit here, we will also die. So come now, let us go over to the camp of the Arameans. If they let us live, we will live; if they kill us, we will die.” (7:4).
So they arose at twilight and went to the camp of the Arameans. But when they came to the outskirts of the camp, there was not a man to be found. (7:5).

For the Lord had caused the Arameans to hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army, so that they said to one another, “Look, the king of Israel must have hired the kings of the Hittites and Egyptians to attack us.” (7:6).
Thus the Arameans had arisen and fled at twilight, abandoning their tents and horses and donkeys. The camp was intact, and they had run for their lives. (7:7).

When the lepers reached the edge of the camp, they went into a tent to eat and drink. Then they carried off the silver, gold, and clothing, and went and hid them. On returning, they entered another tent, carried off some items from there, and hid them. (7:8).

Finally, they said to one another, “We are not doing what is right. Today is a day of good news. If we are silent and wait until morning light, our sin will overtake us. Now, therefore, let us go and tell the king’s household.” (7:9).

So they went and called out to the gatekeepers of the city, saying, “We went to the Aramean camp and no one was there— not a trace — only tethered horses and donkeys, and the tents were intact.” (7:10).
The gatekeepers shouted the news, and it was reported to the king’s household. (7:11).

So the king got up in the night and said to his servants, “Let me tell you what the Arameans have done to us. They know we are starving, so they have left the camp to hide in the field, thinking, ‘When they come out of the city, we will take them alive and enter the city.’” (7:12).

But one of his servants replied, “Please, have scouts take five of the horses that remain in the city. Their plight will be no worse than all the Israelites who are left here. You can see that all the Israelites here are doomed. So let us send them and find out.” (7:13).
Then the scouts took two chariots with horses, and the king sent them after the Aramean army, saying, “Go and see.” (7:14).

And they tracked them as far as the Jordan, and indeed, the whole way was littered with the clothing and equipment the Arameans had thrown off in haste. So the scouts returned and told the king. (7:15).

Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Arameans. It was then that a seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley sold for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD. (7:16).

Now the king had appointed the officer on whose arm he leaned to be in charge of the gate, but the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died, just as the man of God had foretold when the king had come to him. (7:17).

It happened just as the man of God had told the king: “About this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria, two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel, and a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel.” (7:18).

And the officer had answered the man of God, “Look, even if the LORD were to make windows in heaven, could this really happen?” So Elisha had replied, “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it!” (7:19).
And that is just what happened to him. The people trampled him in the gateway, and he died. (7:20).

Deuteronomy 28:7: The LORD will cause your enemies to be struck down before you; they will come out one way and flee before you seven ways.
Judges 7:19-22: Three hundred men blow trumpets and smash jars, and the whole camp panics and turns on itself.

Far more than an entrance; the public square where elders heard legal cases, contracts were witnessed, market business transacted, and news was exchanged. 'Sitting in the gate' (Genesis 19:1; Ruth 4:1-11; Proverbs 31:23) signals civic authority and active community life.

Both a weight (about 0.4 oz / 11 g) and a currency unit. In Old Testament economy a common laborer earned roughly half a shekel per month, so the 20 shekels paid for Joseph (Genesis 37:28) was about three years of wages.
