stories.title: 💧 2 Kings 8
summaryBullets: Now Elisha had said to the woman whose son he had restored to life, “Arise, you and your household; go and live as a foreigner wherever you can. For the LORD has decreed that a seven-year famine will come to the land.” (8:1).
So the woman had proceeded to do as the man of God had instructed. And she and her household lived as foreigners for seven years in the land of the Philistines. (8:2).
At the end of seven years, when the woman returned from the land of the Philistines, she went to the king to appeal for her house and her land. (8:3).
Now the king had been speaking to Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, saying, “Please relate to me all the great things Elisha has done.” (8:4).

And Gehazi was telling the king how Elisha had brought the dead back to life. Just then the woman whose son Elisha had revived came to appeal to the king for her house and her land. So Gehazi said, “My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is the son Elisha restored to life.” (8:5).

When the king asked the woman, she confirmed it. So the king appointed for her an officer, saying, “Restore all that was hers, along with all the proceeds of the field from the day that she left the country until now.” (8:6).
Then Elisha came to Damascus while Ben-hadad king of Aram was sick, and the king was told, “The man of God has come here.” (8:7).
So the king said to Hazael, “Take a gift in your hand, go to meet the man of God, and inquire of the LORD through him, ‘Will I recover from this illness?’” (8:8).

So Hazael went to meet Elisha, taking with him a gift of forty camel loads of every good thing from Damascus. And he went in and stood before him and said, “Your son Ben-hadad king of Aram has sent me to ask, ‘Will I recover from this illness?’” (8:9).
Elisha answered, “Go and tell him, ‘You will surely recover.’ But the LORD has shown me that in fact he will die.” (8:10).
Elisha fixed his gaze steadily on him until Hazael became uncomfortable. Then the man of God began to weep. (8:11).

“Why is my lord weeping?” asked Hazael. “Because I know the evil you will do to the Israelites,” Elisha replied. “You will set fire to their fortresses, kill their young men with the sword, dash their little ones to pieces, and rip open their pregnant women.” (8:12).
“But how could your servant, a mere dog, do such a monstrous thing?” said Hazael. And Elisha answered, “The LORD has shown me that you will be king over Aram.” (8:13).
So Hazael left Elisha and went to his master, who asked him, “What did Elisha say to you?” And he replied, “He told me that you would surely recover.” (8:14).
But the next day Hazael took a thick cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it over the king’s face. So Ben-hadad died, and Hazael reigned in his place. (8:15).
In the fifth year of the reign of Joram son of Ahab over Israel, Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat succeeded his father as king of Judah. (8:16).
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years. (8:17).
And Jehoram walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, just as the house of Ahab had done. For he married a daughter of Ahab and did evil in the sight of the LORD. (8:18).
Yet for the sake of His servant David, the LORD was unwilling to destroy Judah, since He had promised to maintain a lamp for David and his descendants forever. (8:19).
In the days of Jehoram, Edom rebelled against the hand of Judah and appointed their own king. (8:20).
So Jehoram crossed over to Zair with all his chariots. When the Edomites surrounded him and his chariot commanders, he rose up and attacked by night. His troops, however, fled to their homes. (8:21).
So to this day Edom has been in rebellion against the hand of Judah. Likewise, Libnah rebelled at the same time. (8:22).
As for the rest of the acts of Jehoram, along with all his accomplishments, are they not written in the book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (8:23).
And Jehoram rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David. And his son Ahaziah reigned in his place. (8:24).
In the twelfth year of the reign of Joram son of Ahab over Israel, Ahaziah son of Jehoram became king of Judah. (8:25).
Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem one year. His mother’s name was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri king of Israel. (8:26).
And Ahaziah walked in the ways of the house of Ahab and did evil in the sight of the LORD like the house of Ahab, for he was a son-in-law of the house of Ahab. (8:27).
Then Ahaziah went with Joram son of Ahab to fight against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-gilead, and the Arameans wounded Joram. (8:28).

So King Joram returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds that the Arameans had inflicted on him at Ramah when he fought against Hazael king of Aram. Then Ahaziah son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to Jezreel to visit Joram son of Ahab, because Joram had been wounded. (8:29).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 4:8-37: The Shunammite woman, her son given and then raised, the account Gehazi is repeating to the king.
Leviticus 25:23-28: The land is not sold in perpetuity, and a man's holding returns to his family.
1 Kings 19:15-17: Elijah is sent to anoint Hazael king over Aram and Jehu king over Israel.
2 Chronicles 21:1-20: The parallel account of Jehoram of Judah, with Elijah's letter and the disease that killed him.
Genesis 27:40: Esau will live by his sword and serve his brother, but will break his brother's yoke from his neck.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶבֶד (ʿeved), Greek: δοῦλος (doulos), Aramaic: עבדא (ʿavda)
translationNotes.note: Children could be seized as slaves to pay debts. The oil miracle prevented this fate.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צָרַעַת (ṣaraʿat), Greek: λέπρα (lepra), Aramaic: גרבתא (garbata)
translationNotes.note: Not modern Hansen’s disease but a range of skin conditions causing ritual uncleanness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יַרְדֵּן (Yarden), Greek: Ἰορδάνης (Iordanēs), Aramaic: ירדנא (Yardena)
translationNotes.note: River of Israel central to baptismal symbolism and repeated miracles.

Verse 15 has Hazael smother Ben-hadad and take the throne of Damascus, and he becomes Israel's most damaging enemy for forty years. Assyrian records agree that he was a usurper: Shalmaneser III's inscriptions call Hazael a son of a nobody who seized the throne, the standard Assyrian phrase for a king with no royal father.

Verse 1 has Elisha warn the Shunammite to leave the land for seven years. A family that abandoned its fields lost possession of them in practice, which is why she has to petition the king to get her house and land back in verse 3. Land could not be sold away permanently under the law (Leviticus 25:23-28), but recovering it still took a hearing before the crown.

stories.keyTakeaway: A woman whose son Elisha restored to life returns from exile and the king restores her property; Elisha travels to Damascus where he tells Hazael he will become king of Aram and commits atrocities against Israel, and Hazael then suffocates Ben-Hadad to take the throne. In Judah, Jehoram and his son Ahaziah reign and do evil; Edom and Libnah rebel against Judah, and Ahaziah later visits the wounded Joram of Israel.

stories.title: 🗡️ 2 Kings 9
summaryBullets: Now Elisha the prophet summoned one of the sons of the prophets and said to him, “Tuck your cloak under your belt, take this flask of oil, and go to Ramoth-gilead. (9:1).
When you arrive, look for Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi. Go in, get him away from his companions, and take him to an inner room. (9:2).
Then take the flask of oil, pour it on his head, and declare, ‘This is what the LORD says: I anoint you king over Israel.’ Then open the door and run. Do not delay!” (9:3).
So the young prophet went to Ramoth-gilead, (9:4).
and when he arrived, the army commanders were sitting there. “I have a message for you, commander,” he said. “For which of us?” asked Jehu. “For you, commander,” he replied. (9:5).

So Jehu got up and went into the house, where the young prophet poured the oil on his head and declared, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anoint you king over the LORD’s people Israel. (9:6).
And you are to strike down the house of your master Ahab, so that I may avenge the blood of My servants the prophets and the blood of all the servants of the LORD shed by the hand of Jezebel. (9:7).
The whole house of Ahab will perish, and I will cut off from Ahab every male, both slave and free, in Israel. (9:8).
I will make the house of Ahab like the houses of Jeroboam son of Nebat and Baasha son of Ahijah. (9:9).
And on the plot of ground at Jezreel the dogs will devour Jezebel, and there will be no one to bury her.’” Then the young prophet opened the door and ran. (9:10).
When Jehu went out to the servants of his master, they asked, “Is everything all right? Why did this madman come to you?” “You know his kind and their babble,” he replied. (9:11).
“That is a lie!” they said. “Tell us now!” So Jehu answered, “He talked to me about this and that, saying, ‘This is what the LORD says: I anoint you king over Israel.’” (9:12).
Quickly, each man took his garment and put it under Jehu on the bare steps. Then they blew the ram’s horn and proclaimed, “Jehu is king!” (9:13).
Thus Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi, conspired against Joram. (Now Joram and all Israel had been defending Ramoth-gilead against Hazael king of Aram, (9:14).

but King Joram had returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds he had suffered at the hands of the Arameans in the battle against Hazael their king.) So Jehu said, “If you commanders wish to make me king, then do not let anyone escape from the city to go and tell it in Jezreel.” (9:15).
Then Jehu got into his chariot and went to Jezreel, because Joram was laid up there. And Ahaziah king of Judah had gone down to see him. (9:16).

Now the watchman standing on the tower in Jezreel saw Jehu’s troops approaching, and he called out, “I see a company of troops!” “Choose a rider,” Joram commanded. “Send him out to meet them and ask, ‘Have you come in peace?’” (9:17).

So a horseman rode off to meet Jehu and said, “This is what the king asks: ‘Have you come in peace?’” “What do you know about peace?” Jehu replied. “Fall in behind me.” And the watchman reported, “The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back.” (9:18).
So the king sent out a second horseman, who went to them and said, “This is what the king asks: ‘Have you come in peace?’” “What do you know about peace?” Jehu replied. “Fall in behind me.” (9:19).
Again the watchman reported, “He reached them, but he is not coming back. And the charioteer is driving like Jehu son of Nimshi— he is driving like a madman!” (9:20).

“Harness!” Joram shouted, and they harnessed his chariot. Then Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah set out, each in his own chariot, and met Jehu on the property of Naboth the Jezreelite. (9:21).
When Joram saw Jehu, he asked, “Have you come in peace, Jehu?” “How can there be peace,” he replied, “as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel abound?” (9:22).
Joram turned around and fled, calling out to Ahaziah, “Treachery, Ahaziah!” (9:23).
Then Jehu drew his bow and shot Joram between the shoulders. The arrow pierced his heart, and he slumped down in his chariot. (9:24).

And Jehu said to Bidkar his officer, “Pick him up and throw him into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite. For remember that when you and I were riding together behind his father Ahab, the LORD lifted up this burden against him: (9:25).

‘As surely as I saw the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons yesterday, declares the LORD, so will I repay you on this plot of ground, declares the LORD.’ Now then, according to the word of the LORD, pick him up and throw him on the plot of ground.” (9:26).

When King Ahaziah of Judah saw this, he fled up the road toward Beth-haggan. And Jehu pursued him, shouting, “Shoot him too!” So they shot Ahaziah in his chariot on the Ascent of Gur, near Ibleam, and he fled to Megiddo and died there. (9:27).
Then his servants carried him by chariot to Jerusalem and buried him with his fathers in his tomb in the City of David. (9:28).
(In the eleventh year of Joram son of Ahab, Ahaziah had become king over Judah.) (9:29).
Now when Jehu arrived in Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it. So she painted her eyes, adorned her head, and looked down from a window. (9:30).
And as Jehu entered the gate, she asked, “Have you come in peace, O Zimri, murderer of your master?” (9:31).
He looked up at the window and called out, “Who is on my side? Who?” And two or three eunuchs looked down at him. (9:32).
“Throw her down!” yelled Jehu. So they threw her down, and her blood splattered on the wall and on the horses as they trampled her underfoot. (9:33).
Then Jehu went in and ate and drank. “Take care of this cursed woman,” he said, “and bury her, for she was the daughter of a king.” (9:34).
But when they went out to bury her, they found nothing but her skull, her feet, and the palms of her hands. (9:35).

So they went back and told Jehu, who replied, “This is the word of the LORD, which He spoke through His servant Elijah the Tishbite: ‘On the plot of ground at Jezreel the dogs will devour the flesh of Jezebel. (9:36).
And Jezebel’s body will lie like dung in the field on the plot of ground at Jezreel, so that no one can say: This is Jezebel.’” (9:37).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 21:17-24: Elijah's word that dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel and lick up Ahab's blood.
1 Kings 19:16-17: Jehu son of Nimshi is to be anointed king over Israel, and whoever escapes Hazael's sword Jehu will kill.
1 Kings 21:1-16: Naboth is stoned on the word of two paid witnesses so that Ahab can take his vineyard in Jezreel.
2 Chronicles 22:7-9: The parallel account of the death of Ahaziah of Judah at Jehu's hands.
Hosea 1:4-5: I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel and put an end to the kingdom of Israel.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָשַׁח (mashach), to smear with oil
translationNotes.note: Olive oil poured from a flask over the head, the act that installed a man in office and made the appointment public and irreversible. Kings, priests, and on occasion prophets were anointed, and the passive participle of this verb, mashiach, is the word behind messiah. Verses 3 and 6 have it done indoors and in a hurry by a young member of a prophetic guild, because this anointing is a coup against a reigning king.

The men who throw Jezebel from the window in verses 32 and 33 are the officers of her own household. The word covers senior court servants of a royal establishment, and in the surrounding empires men in such posts, especially those with access to the women's quarters, were commonly castrated so they could found no line of their own. Isaiah 56:3-5 addresses the standing of such men in Israel directly.

A royal residence of the northern kings at the eastern end of the great valley that carries its name, the one flat corridor across northern Israel. Ahab had a palace there next to Naboth's vineyard, seized after Jezebel had the man killed by false witnesses (1 Kings 21:1-16). Verses 25 and 26 have Jehu throw Joram's body onto that same plot of ground and say why.

Verse 30 says Jezebel set her eyes in pukh and dressed her head. The paint was ground galena or antimony, black, applied around the eye with a small stick from a pot; jars and applicators turn up in graves all over the region. Doing it before appearing at an upper window is the act of a queen presenting herself in state, not a woman hiding.

Jezebel's greeting in verse 31, 'Have you come in peace, O Zimri, murderer of your master,' names a specific man. Zimri commanded half the chariots, killed King Elah while he was drinking, wiped out the royal house, and held the throne seven days before the army made Omri king and Zimri burned the palace down over himself (1 Kings 16:9-20). She is telling Jehu how long she expects his coup to last.

stories.keyTakeaway: Elisha sends a prophet to anoint Jehu as king of Israel with orders to destroy the house of Ahab; Jehu's army officers proclaim him king, he kills King Joram and chases down King Ahaziah, then throws Jezebel from a window in Jezreel where dogs consume her body.

stories.title: 🗡️ 2 Kings 10
summaryBullets: Now Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. So Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria to the officials of Jezreel, to the elders, and to the guardians of the sons of Ahab, saying: (10:1).
“When this letter arrives, since your master’s sons are with you and you have chariots and horses, a fortified city and weaponry, (10:2).
select the best and most worthy son of your master, set him on his father’s throne, and fight for your master’s house.” (10:3).
But they were terrified and reasoned, “If two kings could not stand against him, how can we?” (10:4).

So the palace administrator, the overseer of the city, the elders, and the guardians sent a message to Jehu: “We are your servants, and we will do whatever you say. We will not make anyone king. Do whatever is good in your sight.” (10:5).

Then Jehu wrote them a second letter and said: “If you are on my side, and if you will obey me, then bring the heads of your master’s sons to me at Jezreel by this time tomorrow.” Now the sons of the king, seventy in all, were being brought up by the leading men of the city. (10:6).
And when the letter arrived, they took the sons of the king and slaughtered all seventy of them. They put their heads in baskets and sent them to Jehu at Jezreel. (10:7).
When the messenger arrived, he told Jehu, “They have brought the heads of the sons of the king.” And Jehu ordered, “Pile them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until morning.” (10:8).
The next morning, Jehu went out and stood before all the people and said, “You are innocent. It was I who conspired against my master and killed him. But who killed all these? (10:9).
Know, then, that not a word the LORD has spoken against the house of Ahab will fail, for the LORD has done what He promised through His servant Elijah.” (10:10).
So Jehu killed everyone in Jezreel who remained of the house of Ahab, as well as all his great men and close friends and priests, leaving him without a single survivor. (10:11).
Then Jehu set out toward Samaria. At Beth-eked of the Shepherds, (10:12).

Jehu met some relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah and asked, “Who are you?” “We are relatives of Ahaziah,” they answered, “and we have come down to greet the sons of the king and of the queen mother.” (10:13).
Then Jehu ordered, “Take them alive.” So his men took them alive, then slaughtered them at the well of Beth-eked— forty-two men. He spared none of them. (10:14).

When he left there, he found Jehonadab son of Rechab, who was coming to meet him. Jehu greeted him and asked, “Is your heart as true to mine as my heart is to yours?” “It is!” Jehonadab replied. “If it is,” said Jehu, “give me your hand.” So he gave him his hand, and Jehu helped him into his chariot, (10:15).
saying, “Come with me and see my zeal for the LORD!” So he had him ride in his chariot. (10:16).
When Jehu came to Samaria, he struck down everyone belonging to Ahab who remained there, until he had destroyed them, according to the word that the LORD had spoken to Elijah. (10:17).
Then Jehu brought all the people together and said, “Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him a lot. (10:18).

Now, therefore, summon to me all the prophets of Baal, all his servants, and all his priests. See that no one is missing, for I have a great sacrifice for Baal. Whoever is missing will not live.” But Jehu was acting deceptively in order to destroy the servants of Baal. (10:19).
And Jehu commanded, “Proclaim a solemn assembly for Baal.” So they announced it. (10:20).
Then Jehu sent word throughout Israel, and all the servants of Baal came; there was not a man who failed to show. They entered the temple of Baal, and it was filled from end to end. (10:21).
And Jehu said to the keeper of the wardrobe, “Bring out garments for all the servants of Baal.” So he brought out garments for them. (10:22).

Next, Jehu and Jehonadab son of Rechab entered the temple of Baal, and Jehu said to the servants of Baal, “Look around to see that there are no servants of the LORD here among you— only servants of Baal.” (10:23).

And they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Now Jehu had stationed eighty men outside and warned them, “If anyone allows one of the men I am delivering into your hands to escape, he will forfeit his life for theirs.” (10:24).

When he had finished making the burnt offering, Jehu said to the guards and officers, “Go in and kill them. Do not let anyone out.” So the guards and officers put them to the sword, threw the bodies out, and went into the inner room of the temple of Baal. (10:25).
They brought out the sacred pillar of the temple of Baal and burned it. (10:26).
They also demolished the sacred pillar of Baal. Then they tore down the temple of Baal and made it into a latrine, which it is to this day. (10:27).
Thus Jehu eradicated Baal from Israel, (10:28).
but he did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit— the worship of the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. (10:29).

Nevertheless, the LORD said to Jehu, “Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in My sight and have done to the house of Ahab all that was in My heart, four generations of your sons will sit on the throne of Israel.” (10:30).
Yet Jehu was not careful to follow the instruction of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit. (10:31).
In those days the LORD began to reduce the size of Israel. Hazael defeated the Israelites throughout their territory (10:32).
from the Jordan eastward through all the land of Gilead (the region of Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh), and from Aroer by the Arnon Valley through Gilead to Bashan. (10:33).
As for the rest of the acts of Jehu, along with all his accomplishments and all his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? (10:34).
And Jehu rested with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and his son Jehoahaz reigned in his place. (10:35).
So the duration of Jehu’s reign over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years. (10:36).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 21:21-22: God will cut off from Ahab every male and make his house like the house of Jeroboam and of Baasha.
Deuteronomy 13:12-18: A town that turns aside to serve other gods is to be struck down and its spoil burned in the open square.
Jeremiah 35:1-19: The Rechabites, sons of Jonadab, keep his command to drink no wine, build no house, and live in tents.
Hosea 1:4-5: I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel and break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel.
1 Kings 12:28-30: Jeroboam's calves at Bethel and Dan, which verse 29 says Jehu never turned away from.

translationNotes.note: Verse 29 records the limit of Jehu's reform: he destroyed Baal but left the calves Jeroboam had set at Bethel and at Dan. Those two shrines were state policy from the day the kingdom split, put at the southern and northern ends of the country so no Israelite needed to travel to Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:26-30). A large stepped platform for such a sanctuary has been excavated at Tel Dan.

Verses 7 and 8 have seventy heads sent to Jehu in baskets and stacked in two heaps at the city gate until morning. Displaying the heads of a defeated house at the gate was normal Assyrian and Near Eastern practice, meant to be seen by everyone entering and leaving. The gate was where the town's public business happened, so the heap was addressed to the whole population of Jezreel.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית עֵקֶד (Bet Eqed), house of binding
translationNotes.note: The place in verses 12 to 14 where forty-two of Ahaziah's relatives are killed at the well. The name comes from the verb for binding, the same root used when Abraham bound Isaac (Genesis 22:9), and it names the pen where shepherds tied sheep for shearing. It sat on the road from Jezreel up to Samaria, a working sheep station with water, which is why travellers stopped there.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְהוֹנָדָב בֶּן רֵכָב (Yehonadav ben Rekhav)
translationNotes.note: The man Jehu pulls up into his chariot in verses 15 and 16 is the founder of a clan whose rule survived for centuries. Jeremiah 35 records his descendants refusing wine in the temple itself because Jonadab had commanded them to drink none, build no house, sow no seed, and live in tents all their days. Taking him aboard put a recognised name for austerity beside a new king.

translationNotes.term: The temple of Baal made a latrine
translationNotes.note: Verses 18 to 27 describe the trap: a summoned assembly, robes handed out at the door by the keeper of the wardrobe so no worshipper of the LORD could be mistaken for a servant of Baal, eighty men posted outside, and the killing done once the offering was finished. The building was then pulled down and the site turned into a public latrine, which made it permanently unusable for worship.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jehu eliminates Ahab's entire house and their allies through a campaign of deception and slaughter, then destroys Baal worship in Israel by tricking Baal's servants into the temple and executing them; God promises his descendants will rule for four generations, though Jehu continues Israel's worship of golden calves and the kingdom begins to shrink under Hazael's attacks.

headings.text: Jehu Kills the Priests of Baal

stories.title: 👑 2 Kings 11
summaryBullets: When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she proceeded to annihilate all the royal heirs. (11:1).

But Jehosheba daughter of King Joram, the sister of Ahaziah, took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the sons of the king who were being murdered. She put him and his nurse in a bedroom to hide him from Athaliah, and he was not killed. (11:2).
And Joash remained hidden with his nurse in the house of the LORD for six years while Athaliah ruled the land. (11:3).

Then in the seventh year, Jehoiada sent for the commanders of hundreds, the Carites, and the guards, and had them brought into the house of the LORD. There he made a covenant with them and put them under oath. He showed them the king’s son (11:4).
and commanded them, “This is what you are to do: A third of you who come on duty on the Sabbath shall guard the royal palace, (11:5).
a third shall be at the gate of Sur, and a third at the gate behind the guards. You are to take turns guarding the temple — (11:6).
the two divisions that would go off duty on the Sabbath are to guard the house of the LORD for the king. (11:7).
You must surround the king with weapons in hand, and anyone who approaches the ranks must be put to death. You must stay close to the king wherever he goes.” (11:8).

So the commanders of hundreds did everything that Jehoiada the priest had ordered. Each of them took his men— those coming on duty on the Sabbath and those going off duty— and came to Jehoiada the priest. (11:9).
Then the priest gave to the commanders of hundreds the spears and shields of King David from the house of the LORD. (11:10).
And the guards stood with weapons in hand surrounding the king by the altar and the temple, from the south side to the north side of the temple. (11:11).

Then Jehoiada brought out the king’s son, put the crown on him, presented him with the Testimony, and proclaimed him king. They anointed him, and the people clapped their hands and declared, “Long live the king!” (11:12).
When Athaliah heard the noise from the guards and the people, she went out to the people in the house of the LORD. (11:13).

And she looked out and saw the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom. The officers and trumpeters were beside the king, and all the people of the land were rejoicing and blowing trumpets. Then Athaliah tore her clothes and screamed, “Treason! Treason!” (11:14).

And Jehoiada the priest ordered the commanders of hundreds in charge of the army, “Bring her out between the ranks, and put to the sword anyone who follows her.” For the priest had said, “She must not be put to death in the house of the LORD.” (11:15).
So they seized Athaliah as she reached the horses’ entrance to the palace grounds, and there she was put to death. (11:16).
Then Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people that they would be the LORD’s people. He also made a covenant between the king and the people. (11:17).

So all the people of the land went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They smashed the altars and idols to pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal in front of the altars. And Jehoiada the priest posted guards for the house of the LORD. (11:18).

He took with him the commanders of hundreds, the Carites, the guards, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD and entered the royal palace by way of the Gate of the Guards. Then Joash took his seat on the royal throne, (11:19).
and all the people of the land rejoiced. And the city was quiet, because Athaliah had been put to the sword at the royal palace. (11:20).
Joash was seven years old when he became king. (11:21).
crossRefs: 2 Chronicles 22:10-23:21: The same coup, told with the Levites, the priestly divisions, and the singers set out in full.
2 Samuel 7:12-16: The oath that David's house, kingdom, and throne would be made sure forever.
Deuteronomy 17:18-20: The king is to write out his own copy of the law and read it all the days of his life.
1 Kings 16:31-33: Ahab marries Jezebel, serves Baal, and builds him a house and an altar in Samaria.
Deuteronomy 13:6-11: Anyone who entices you to serve other gods is to be put to death, and the hand of the witness is first against him.

translationNotes.note: Verse 12 has Jehoiada put the crown on the boy and give him the edut. The word means the covenant terms in written form, and it is used of the tablets inside the ark (Exodus 25:16). Deuteronomy 17:18-20 requires a king of Israel to have his own copy of the law written out and to read it all his life, so handing it over at the coronation put the crown under the document.

Verse 17 records two covenants made the same day, one between the LORD and the king and people, and one between the king and the people. Kingship in Judah was contractual in this second sense from the beginning; the elders cut a covenant with David at Hebron before anointing him (2 Samuel 5:3). The tearing down of Baal's temple in the next verse follows from the first.

The troops Jehoiada brings into the plot in verses 4 and 19, listed beside the palace runners. They were a foreign mercenary corps serving as the royal bodyguard, the same arrangement David used with the Cherethites and Pelethites and with six hundred men from Gath (2 Samuel 8:18, 15:18). Foreign guards had no clan loyalties inside the kingdom, which is exactly why kings hired them.

translationNotes.term: The spears and shields of King David
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲנִית (hanit), spear - שֶׁלֶט (shelet), small shield
translationNotes.note: Verse 10 arms the guard from the temple stores. Weapons captured in war were dedicated to the sanctuary and hung there rather than reissued; David sent in the gold shields taken from Hadadezer's men (2 Samuel 8:7-11), and Goliath's sword was kept behind the ephod at Nob (1 Samuel 21:9). Jehoiada takes century-old trophies off the wall to equip a coup.

Verses 15 and 16 have Jehoiada order Athaliah brought out of the temple precinct before she is killed, and she is put to death at the gate where horses entered the palace grounds. Blood shed in the sanctuary would have defiled it (Numbers 35:33-34), and the priest is explicit that she must not die in the house of the LORD. The detail is procedural, not incidental.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jehosheba hides the young king Joash from his grandmother Athaliah, who murders the royal family; six years later Jehoiada the priest orchestrates a coup, crowns and anoints Joash, executes Athaliah, and tears down the temple of Baal.

headings.text: Jehoiada Restores the Worship of the Lord

stories.title: 👑 2 Kings 12
summaryBullets: In the seventh year of Jehu, Joash became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem forty years. His mother’s name was Zibiah; she was from Beersheba. (12:1).
And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days he was instructed by Jehoiada the priest. (12:2).
Nevertheless, the high places were not removed; the people continued sacrificing and burning incense there. (12:3).

Then Joash said to the priests, “Collect all the money brought as sacred gifts into the house of the LORD — the census money, the money from vows, and the money brought voluntarily into the house of the LORD. (12:4).
Let every priest receive it from his constituency, and let it be used to repair any damage found in the temple.” (12:5).
By the twenty-third year of the reign of Joash, however, the priests had not yet repaired the damage to the temple. (12:6).

So King Joash called Jehoiada and the other priests and said, “Why have you not repaired the damage to the temple? Now, therefore, take no more money from your constituency, but hand it over for the repair of the temple.” (12:7).
So the priests agreed that they would not receive money from the people and that they would not repair the temple themselves. (12:8).

Then Jehoiada the priest took a chest, bored a hole in its lid, and set it beside the altar on the right side as one enters the house of the LORD. There the priests who guarded the threshold put all the money brought into the house of the LORD. (12:9).

Whenever they saw that there was a large amount of money in the chest, the royal scribe and the high priest would go up, count the money brought into the house of the LORD, and tie it up in bags. (12:10).
Then they would put the counted money into the hands of those who supervised the work on the house of the LORD, who in turn would pay those doing the work — the carpenters, builders, (12:11).
masons, and stonecutters. They also purchased timber and dressed stone to repair the damage to the house of the LORD, and they paid the other expenses of the temple repairs. (12:12).

However, the money brought into the house of the LORD was not used for making silver basins, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, trumpets, or any articles of gold or silver for the house of the LORD. (12:13).
Instead, it was paid to those doing the work, and with it they repaired the house of the LORD. (12:14).
No accounting was required from the men who received the money to pay the workmen, because they acted with integrity. (12:15).
The money from the guilt offerings and sin offerings was not brought into the house of the LORD; it belonged to the priests. (12:16).
At that time Hazael king of Aram marched up and fought against Gath and captured it. Then he decided to attack Jerusalem. (12:17).

So King Joash of Judah took all the sacred objects dedicated by his fathers— Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, the kings of Judah— along with his own consecrated items and all the gold found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace, and he sent them to Hazael king of Aram. So Hazael withdrew from Jerusalem. (12:18).
As for the rest of the acts of Joash, along with all his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (12:19).
And the servants of Joash rose up and formed a conspiracy and killed him at Beth-millo, on the road down to Silla. (12:20).

His servants Jozabad son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer struck him down, and he died. And they buried him with his fathers in the City of David, and his son Amaziah reigned in his place. (12:21).
crossRefs: Exodus 30:11-16: Every man twenty years old and over gives a half shekel as a ransom for his life when he is counted.
Leviticus 5:14-16: The guilt offering, with restitution paid and a fifth added, given to the priest.
2 Chronicles 24:4-14: The same repair, with the chest set outside the gate and a proclamation to bring in the tax of Moses.
2 Chronicles 24:17-22: After Jehoiada dies, Joash turns away and has Zechariah the priest's son stoned in the temple court.
Matthew 23:35: The blood of Zechariah, murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.

translationNotes.term: The three kinds of temple money
translationNotes.note: Verse 4 names three separate revenues. The census money is the half shekel every man of twenty and over paid for the service of the sanctuary, the same amount from rich and poor alike (Exodus 30:11-16). The vow money is the fixed valuation paid when a person was dedicated and then redeemed, fifty shekels for a man aged twenty to sixty and thirty for a woman (Leviticus 27:1-8). The third is whatever anyone chose to give.

The phrase translated as damage or repairs literally names the cracks and breaches in the fabric. The same word is used of a ship's seams in Ezekiel 27:9, where Tyre's caulkers are 'the repairers of your bedeq.' The chapter is about a building a hundred and fifty years old with holes in it, and money that kept arriving without any of them being closed.

translationNotes.term: A chest with a hole in the lid
translationNotes.note: For twenty-three years the priests collected the repair money themselves and nothing got repaired (verses 6 and 7). Jehoiada's fix in verse 9 was mechanical: one chest, a hole bored in the lid, set beside the altar where every worshipper walked past, and the money counted by the king's secretary and the high priest together. Verse 15 says no accounting was required of the foremen, because they dealt honestly.

translationNotes.term: Paying an army to go away
translationNotes.note: Verses 17 and 18 have Hazael of Aram take Gath and turn toward Jerusalem, and Joash empty the temple and palace treasuries, including gifts dedicated by three earlier kings, to buy him off. Buying an invader off was ordinary and expensive statecraft: Hezekiah does the same with Sennacherib for three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold (2 Kings 18:14-16). It is why the temple treasury keeps being stripped.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית מִלּוֹא (Bet Millo), house of the filling
translationNotes.note: The place in verse 20 where the king's own servants kill him. The Millo was the earthwork holding up the eastern slope of the City of David, packed earth and stone behind retaining walls to make level ground on a steep hillside, built up by David and repaired by later kings (2 Samuel 5:9, 1 Kings 9:15, 2 Chronicles 32:5). Beth-millo names the structure standing on it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joash becomes king and does right under Jehoiada's guidance, instituting a chest system to collect temple donations and funding repairs; later he pays tribute to Hazael of Aram and is assassinated by his officials.

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Kings 13
summaryBullets: In the twenty-third year of the reign of Joash son of Ahaziah over Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria seventeen years. (13:1).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD and followed the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit; he did not turn away from them. (13:2).
So the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He delivered them continually into the hands of Hazael king of Aram and his son Ben-hadad. (13:3).
Then Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD, and the LORD listened to him because He saw the oppression that the king of Aram had inflicted on Israel. (13:4).
So the LORD gave Israel a deliverer, and they escaped the power of the Arameans. Then the people of Israel lived in their own homes as they had before. (13:5).

Nevertheless, they did not turn away from the sins that the house of Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit, but they continued to walk in them. The Asherah pole even remained standing in Samaria. (13:6).
Jehoahaz had no army left, except fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers, because the king of Aram had destroyed them and made them like the dust at threshing. (13:7).
As for the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz, along with all his accomplishments and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? (13:8).
And Jehoahaz rested with his fathers and was buried in Samaria. And his son Jehoash reigned in his place. (13:9).
In the thirty-seventh year of the reign of Joash over Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king of Israel in Samaria, and he reigned sixteen years. (13:10).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not turn away from all the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit, but he walked in them. (13:11).

As for the rest of the acts of Jehoash, along with all his accomplishments and his might, including his war against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? (13:12).
And Jehoash rested with his fathers, and Jeroboam succeeded him on the throne. Jehoash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel. (13:13).

When Elisha had fallen sick with the illness from which he would die, Jehoash king of Israel came down to him and wept over him, saying, “My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!” (13:14).
Elisha told him, “Take a bow and some arrows.” So Jehoash took a bow and some arrows. (13:15).
Then Elisha said to the king of Israel, “Put your hand on the bow.” So the king put his hand on the bow, and Elisha put his hands on the king’s hands. (13:16).

“Open the east window,” said Elisha. So he opened it and Elisha said, “Shoot!” So he shot. And Elisha declared: “This is the LORD’s arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram, for you shall strike the Arameans in Aphek until you have put an end to them.” (13:17).
Then Elisha said, “Take the arrows!” So he took them, and Elisha said to the king of Israel, “Strike the ground!” So he struck the ground three times and stopped. (13:18).

But the man of God was angry with him and said, “You should have struck the ground five or six times. Then you would have struck down Aram until you had put an end to it. But now you will strike down Aram only three times.” (13:19).
And Elisha died and was buried. Now the Moabite raiders used to come into the land every spring. (13:20).

Once, as the Israelites were burying a man, suddenly they saw a band of raiders, so they threw the man’s body into Elisha’s tomb. And as soon as his body touched the bones of Elisha, the man was revived and stood up on his feet. (13:21).
And Hazael king of Aram oppressed Israel throughout the reign of Jehoahaz. (13:22).

But the LORD was gracious to Israel and had compassion on them, and He turned toward them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And to this day, the LORD has been unwilling to destroy them or cast them from His presence. (13:23).
When Hazael king of Aram died, his son Ben-hadad reigned in his place. (13:24).

Then Jehoash son of Jehoahaz took back from Ben-hadad son of Hazael the cities that Hazael had taken in battle from his father Jehoahaz. Jehoash defeated Ben-hadad three times, and so recovered the cities of Israel. (13:25).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 19:15-18: Elijah is told to anoint Hazael and Jehu, and that seven thousand in Israel have not bowed to Baal.
Judges 2:16-19: The LORD raised up judges who saved them, and they turned back and behaved worse than their fathers.
2 Kings 8:11-13: Elisha weeps and tells Hazael the evil he will do to Israel's fortresses, young men, and children.
Exodus 32:13: Moses appeals to the oath God swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, the ground of the mercy in verse 23.
2 Kings 2:9-15: Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit and takes up the cloak that fell from him.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֶכֶב יִשְׂרָאֵל וּפָרָשָׁיו (rekhev Yisrael u-farashav)
translationNotes.note: The cry in verse 14 over the dying Elisha is a military phrase: chariotry and cavalry were the strike arm no hill kingdom could easily field, and the standard measure of a nation's power. Elisha himself had shouted the same words as Elijah was taken up (2 Kings 2:12). A king with fifty horsemen left in his army is calling one man the armoured force of Israel.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵץ תְּשׁוּעָה (hets teshuah), arrow of deliverance
translationNotes.note: Verses 15 to 19 record a prophetic sign carried out with the hands, not a superstition. The prophet's hands go on the king's hands, the east window is opened toward Aramean territory, and the shot is declared over Aphek before the campaign. When the king then strikes the ground three times instead of five or six, the sign is measured out to match, and the outcome in verse 25 is three victories.

The town named in verse 17 as the place of the coming victory sits east of the Sea of Galilee, on the road running down from Damascus into Israelite territory. Ahab had already beaten Ben-hadad's army there once (1 Kings 20:26-30). Naming the ground in advance told the king where the Aramean advance would be broken.

Verse 7 measures how far Israel had fallen: Hazael had left Jehoahaz an army of fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers. Ahab had put two thousand chariots into the field at Qarqar a century earlier, according to Shalmaneser III's own account of that battle. Aram had not conquered Israel; it had simply stripped it of everything that could fight back.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֹּא הַשָּׁנָה (bo ha-shanah), the turn of the year
translationNotes.note: Verse 20 says Moabite raiders came into the land every spring. Campaigning had a season: the winter rains made the tracks impassable and there was nothing in the fields, so armies and raiders moved once the ground dried and the grain was standing, which is what 2 Samuel 11:1 means by the time when kings go out to battle. Verse 21 describes a burial party caught by exactly such a band.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jehoahaz reigns in Israel doing evil, and though he sought the LORD's favor and gained relief from Aramean oppression, Israel continued in idolatry; his son Jehoash then reigned and also did evil, but before dying Elisha prophesied to him about defeating Aram three times, which Jehoash later accomplished by recapturing towns from Ben-Hadad.

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Kings 14
summaryBullets: In the second year of the reign of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz over Israel, Amaziah son of Joash became king of Judah. (14:1).
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Jehoaddan; she was from Jerusalem. (14:2).
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, but not as his father David had done. He did everything as his father Joash had done. (14:3).
Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away, and the people continued sacrificing and burning incense on the high places. (14:4).
As soon as the kingdom was firmly in his grasp, Amaziah executed the servants who had murdered his father the king. (14:5).

Yet he did not put the sons of the murderers to death, but acted according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, where the LORD commanded: “Fathers must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin.” (14:6).
Amaziah struck down 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt. He took Sela in battle and called it Joktheel, which is its name to this very day. (14:7).
Then Amaziah sent messengers to the king of Israel Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, the son of Jehu. “Come, let us meet face to face,” he said. (14:8).

But Jehoash king of Israel replied to Amaziah king of Judah: “A thistle in Lebanon sent a message to a cedar in Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son in marriage.’ Then a wild beast in Lebanon came along and trampled the thistle. (14:9).
You have indeed defeated Edom, and your heart has become proud. Glory in that and stay at home. Why should you stir up trouble so that you fall— you and Judah with you?” (14:10).
But Amaziah would not listen, so Jehoash king of Israel advanced. He and King Amaziah of Judah faced each other at Beth-shemesh in Judah. (14:11).
And Judah was routed before Israel, and every man fled to his home. (14:12).

There at Beth-shemesh, Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Joash, the son of Ahaziah. Then Jehoash went to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate — a section of four hundred cubits. (14:13).
He took all the gold and silver and all the articles found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace, as well as some hostages. Then he returned to Samaria. (14:14).

As for the rest of the acts of Jehoash, along with his accomplishments, his might, and how he waged war against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? (14:15).
And Jehoash rested with his fathers and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel. And his son Jeroboam reigned in his place. (14:16).
Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived for fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel. (14:17).
As for the rest of the acts of Amaziah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (14:18).
And conspirators plotted against Amaziah in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But men were sent after him to Lachish, and they killed him there. (14:19).
They carried him back on horses and buried him in Jerusalem with his fathers in the City of David. (14:20).
Then all the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah. (14:21).
Azariah was the one who rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah after King Amaziah rested with his fathers. (14:22).
In the fifteenth year of the reign of Amaziah son of Joash over Judah, Jeroboam son of Jehoash became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria forty-one years. (14:23).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not turn away from all the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit. (14:24).

This Jeroboam restored the boundary of Israel from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word that the LORD, the God of Israel, had spoken through His servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher. (14:25).
For the LORD saw that the affliction of the Israelites, both slave and free, was very bitter. There was no one to help Israel, (14:26).
and since the LORD had said that He would not blot out the name of Israel from under heaven, He saved them by the hand of Jeroboam son of Jehoash. (14:27).

As for the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, along with all his accomplishments and might, and how he waged war and recovered both Damascus and Hamath for Israel from Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? (14:28).
And Jeroboam rested with his fathers, the kings of Israel. And his son Zechariah reigned in his place. (14:29).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 24:16: Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each dies for his own sin.
Judges 9:7-15: Jotham's parable of the trees, in which the bramble invites the cedars of Lebanon into its shade.
2 Chronicles 25:1-28: The parallel account of Amaziah, with the hired Israelite troops sent home and the gods of Edom.
Jonah 1:1-2: The word of the LORD comes to Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet named in verse 25 of this chapter.
Amos 6:13-14: Those who rejoice over Lo-debar and boast of taking Karnaim, in the days when Israel's border was widest.

translationNotes.term: Fathers shall not be put to death
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 has the king execute his father's assassins but spare their sons, and the text says outright that he acted according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, then quotes it. The quotation is Deuteronomy 24:16. Killing a traitor's whole family was the normal practice of the period, so the verse is recording a king declining to do the ordinary thing because a written law forbade it.

The salt flats at the southern end of the Dead Sea, in the rift valley below sea level, on the boundary between Judah and Edom. It is bare, hot, and open, which makes it usable ground for a set battle in country that otherwise has none. David's men had fought Edom there too and struck down eighteen thousand (1 Chronicles 18:12).

Verse 7 takes a fortress called Sela and renames it Joktheel. Sela simply means the rock, and it was an Edomite stronghold in the highlands south of the Dead Sea, the kind of site reached through a cleft in the cliffs and defended by the terrain rather than by walls. The later Nabataean capital in that same region carries the Greek word for rock as its name, Petra.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָשָׁל (mashal), a saying or fable
translationNotes.note: Verse 9 answers a challenge with a short fable: a thistle in Lebanon demands a cedar's daughter for its son, and a passing animal treads the thistle flat. Scripture has few of these; the other is Jotham's parable of the trees who ask the bramble to reign over them (Judges 9:7-15). The insult is in the casting, and Amaziah reads it correctly.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית שֶׁמֶשׁ (Bet Shemesh), house of the sun
translationNotes.note: The town in verse 11 sits in the Sorek Valley about fifteen miles west of Jerusalem, on the border between Judah and Philistine country; it is where the cart carrying the ark came back from Philistine hands (1 Samuel 6:12-15). After winning there, the king of Israel broke down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall, about six hundred feet, between the Ephraim Gate and the Corner Gate, and left the capital open.

The Dead Sea, named for the Arabah, the rift valley running from the Sea of Galilee down past it to the Gulf of Aqaba. Its surface lies more than 1,300 feet below sea level, the lowest dry land on earth, and its water is about ten times as salty as the ocean, so nothing lives in it. Verse 25 uses it as the southern marker of the border Jeroboam restored, from Lebo-hamath in the far north down to this sea.

stories.keyTakeaway: Amaziah reigns in Judah, defeats Edom, but ignores Jehoash's warning and is defeated in battle; Jehoash captures him, plunders Jerusalem, and later Amaziah is killed in a conspiracy. Meanwhile Jeroboam becomes king of Israel and restores its northern and eastern boundaries.

headings.text: Jeroboam II Succeeds Jehoash in Israel

stories.title: ⚖️ 2 Kings 15
summaryBullets: In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam’s reign over Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah became king of Judah. (15:1).
He was sixteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem fifty-two years. His mother’s name was Jecoliah; she was from Jerusalem. (15:2).
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Amaziah had done. (15:3).
Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away; the people continued sacrificing and burning incense there. (15:4).
And the LORD afflicted the king with leprosy until the day he died, so that he lived in a separate house while his son Jotham had charge of the palace and governed the people of the land. (15:5).
As for the rest of the acts of Azariah, along with all his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (15:6).
And Azariah rested with his fathers and was buried near them in the City of David. And his son Jotham reigned in his place. (15:7).
In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah’s reign over Judah, Zechariah son of Jeroboam became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria six months. (15:8).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done. He did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit. (15:9).
Then Shallum son of Jabesh conspired against Zechariah, struck him down and killed him in front of the people, and reigned in his place. (15:10).
As for the rest of the acts of Zechariah, they are indeed written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. (15:11).
So the word of the LORD spoken to Jehu was fulfilled: “Four generations of your sons will sit on the throne of Israel.” (15:12).
In the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah’s reign over Judah, Shallum son of Jabesh became king, and he reigned in Samaria one full month. (15:13).
Then Menahem son of Gadi went up from Tirzah to Samaria, struck down and killed Shallum son of Jabesh, and reigned in his place. (15:14).
As for the rest of the acts of Shallum, along with the conspiracy he led, they are indeed written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. (15:15).

At that time Menahem, starting from Tirzah, attacked Tiphsah and everyone in its vicinity, because they would not open their gates. So he attacked Tiphsah and ripped open all the pregnant women. (15:16).
In the thirty-ninth year of Azariah’s reign over Judah, Menahem son of Gadi became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria ten years. (15:17).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and throughout his reign he did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit. (15:18).
Then Pul king of Assyria invaded the land, and Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver in order to gain his support and strengthen his own grip on the kingdom. (15:19).

Menahem exacted this money from each of the wealthy men of Israel — fifty shekels of silver from each man — to give to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria withdrew and did not remain in the land. (15:20).
As for the rest of the acts of Menahem, along with all his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? (15:21).
And Menahem rested with his fathers, and his son Pekahiah reigned in his place. (15:22).
In the fiftieth year of Azariah’s reign over Judah, Pekahiah son of Menahem became king of Israel and reigned in Samaria two years. (15:23).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit. (15:24).

Then his officer, Pekah son of Remaliah, conspired against him along with Argob, Arieh, and fifty men of Gilead. And at the citadel of the king’s palace in Samaria, Pekah struck down and killed Pekahiah and reigned in his place. (15:25).
As for the rest of the acts of Pekahiah, along with all his accomplishments, they are indeed written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. (15:26).
In the fifty-second year of Azariah’s reign over Judah, Pekah son of Remaliah became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria twenty years. (15:27).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit. (15:28).

In the days of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, including all the land of Naphtali, and he took the people as captives to Assyria. (15:29).
Then Hoshea son of Elah led a conspiracy against Pekah son of Remaliah. In the twentieth year of Jotham son of Uzziah, Hoshea attacked Pekah, killed him, and reigned in his place. (15:30).
As for the rest of the acts of Pekah, along with all his accomplishments, they are indeed written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. (15:31).
In the second year of the reign of Pekah son of Remaliah over Israel, Jotham son of Uzziah became king of Judah. (15:32).
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years. His mother’s name was Jerusha daughter of Zadok. (15:33).
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Uzziah had done. (15:34).
Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away; the people continued sacrificing and burning incense there. Jotham rebuilt the Upper Gate of the house of the LORD. (15:35).
As for the rest of the acts of Jotham, along with his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (15:36).
(In those days the LORD began to send Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah.) (15:37).
And Jotham rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David his father. And his son Ahaz reigned in his place. (15:38).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 10:30: Jehu is promised that his sons to the fourth generation will sit on the throne of Israel.
2 Chronicles 26:16-21: Uzziah burns incense in the temple, is struck with leprosy on his forehead, and lives in a separate house.

The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

About 75 lbs (34 kg) of metal. A 'talent of gold' in the Old Testament (e.g. 2 Samuel 12:30) refers to physical mass rather than coined currency. The bronze for the Tabernacle (Exodus 38:29) was 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

Verses 19 and 20 have Menahem hand Assyria a thousand talents of silver, raised at fifty shekels from each wealthy man. Exodus 38:25-26 shows a talent is three thousand shekels, so a thousand talents is three million shekels and the levy fell on sixty thousand men. By weight it is roughly thirty-seven tons of silver, paid to keep an Assyrian army from marching.

This chapter dates each king by the year of the king in the other kingdom, and the numbers only line up once three practices are allowed for. Judah began the regnal year in the autumn month Tishri and Israel in the spring month Nisan; one kingdom counted a king's partial first year and the other called it a year of accession; and a son often ruled alongside his father for years, as Jotham does here while Azariah lives in isolation (verse 5). Edwin Thiele set the systems out in The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings in 1951 and reconciled the synchronisms on that basis.

stories.keyTakeaway: Azariah reigns in Judah for fifty-two years doing right before God afflicts him with leprosy; meanwhile in Israel, four kings rise and fall rapidly - Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, and Pekahiah - each assassinated or conquered, with Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria deporting Israelites from the north. Jotham then becomes king of Judah and does what is right, while Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel begin moving against Judah.

stories.title: ⚖️ 2 Kings 16
summaryBullets: In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham became king of Judah. (16:1).
Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years. And unlike David his father, he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God. (16:2).
Instead, he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and even sacrificed his son in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites. (16:3).
And he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree. (16:4).
Then Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to wage war against Jerusalem. They besieged Ahaz but could not overcome him. (16:5).
At that time Rezin king of Aram recovered Elath for Aram, drove out the men of Judah, and sent the Edomites into Elath, where they live to this day. (16:6).

So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me from the hands of the kings of Aram and Israel, who are rising up against me.” (16:7).
Ahaz also took the silver and gold found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king’s palace, and he sent it as a gift to the king of Assyria. (16:8).
So the king of Assyria responded to him, marched up to Damascus, and captured it. He took its people to Kir as captives and put Rezin to death. (16:9).

Then King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria. On seeing the altar in Damascus, King Ahaz sent Uriah the priest a model of the altar and complete plans for its construction. (16:10).
And Uriah the priest built the altar according to all the instructions King Ahaz had sent from Damascus, and he completed it before King Ahaz returned. (16:11).
When the king came back from Damascus and saw the altar, he approached it and presented offerings on it. (16:12).
He offered his burnt offering and his grain offering, poured out his drink offering, and splattered the blood of his peace offerings on the altar. (16:13).
He also took the bronze altar that stood before the LORD from the front of the temple (between the new altar and the house of the LORD) and he put it on the north side of the new altar. (16:14).

Then King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, “Offer on the great altar the morning burnt offering, the evening grain offering, and the king’s burnt offering and grain offering, as well as the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings of all the people of the land. Splatter on the altar all the blood of the burnt offerings and sacrifices. But I will use the bronze altar to seek guidance.” (16:15).
So Uriah the priest did just as King Ahaz had commanded. (16:16).

King Ahaz also cut off the frames of the movable stands and removed the bronze basin from each of them. He took down the Sea from the bronze oxen that were under it and put it on a stone base. (16:17).
And on account of the king of Assyria, he removed the Sabbath canopy they had built in the temple and closed the royal entryway outside the house of the LORD. (16:18).
As for the rest of the acts of Ahaz, along with his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (16:19).
And Ahaz rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David, and his son Hezekiah reigned in his place. (16:20).

Verse 8 sends the silver and gold of the temple and the palace with the request, and Assyria did answer, taking Damascus and killing Rezin.

stories.title: 💔 2 Kings 17
summaryBullets: In the twelfth year of the reign of Ahaz over Judah, Hoshea son of Elah became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria nine years. (17:1).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, but not like the kings of Israel who preceded him. (17:2).
Shalmaneser king of Assyria attacked him, and Hoshea became his vassal and paid him tribute. (17:3).

But the king of Assyria discovered that Hoshea had conspired to send envoys to King So of Egypt, and that he had not paid tribute to the king of Assyria as in previous years. Therefore the king of Assyria arrested Hoshea and put him in prison. (17:4).
Then the king of Assyria invaded the whole land, marched up to Samaria, and besieged it for three years. (17:5).

In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried away the Israelites to Assyria, where he settled them in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes. (17:6).

All this happened because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt. They had worshiped other gods (17:7).
and walked in the customs of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites, as well as in the practices introduced by the kings of Israel. (17:8).
The Israelites secretly did things against the LORD their God that were not right. From watchtower to fortified city, they built high places in all their cities. (17:9).
They set up for themselves sacred pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree. (17:10).
They burned incense on all the high places like the nations that the LORD had driven out before them. They did wicked things, provoking the LORD to anger. (17:11).
They served idols, although the LORD had told them, “You shall not do this thing.” (17:12).

Yet through all His prophets and seers, the LORD warned Israel and Judah, saying, “Turn from your wicked ways and keep My commandments and statutes, according to the entire Law that I commanded your fathers and delivered to you through My servants the prophets.” (17:13).
But they would not listen, and they stiffened their necks like their fathers, who did not believe the LORD their God. (17:14).

They rejected His statutes and the covenant He had made with their fathers, as well as the decrees He had given them. They pursued worthless idols and became worthless themselves, going after the surrounding nations that the LORD had commanded them not to imitate. (17:15).
They abandoned all the commandments of the LORD their God and made for themselves two cast idols of calves and an Asherah pole. They bowed down to all the host of heaven and served Baal. (17:16).
They sacrificed their sons and daughters in the fire and practiced divination and soothsaying. They devoted themselves to doing evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger. (17:17).
So the LORD was very angry with Israel, and He removed them from His presence. Only the tribe of Judah remained, (17:18).
and even Judah did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God, but lived according to the customs Israel had introduced. (17:19).
So the LORD rejected all the descendants of Israel. He afflicted them and delivered them into the hands of plunderers, until He had banished them from His presence. (17:20).
When the LORD had torn Israel away from the house of David, they made Jeroboam son of Nebat king, and Jeroboam led Israel away from following the LORD and caused them to commit a great sin. (17:21).
The Israelites persisted in all the sins that Jeroboam had committed and did not turn away from them. (17:22).

Finally, the LORD removed Israel from His presence, as He had declared through all His servants the prophets. So Israel was exiled from their homeland into Assyria, where they are to this day. (17:23).

Then the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and settled them in the towns of Samaria to replace the Israelites. They took possession of Samaria and lived in its towns. (17:24).
Now when the settlers first lived there, they did not worship the LORD, so He sent lions among them, which killed some of them. (17:25).

So they spoke to the king of Assyria, saying, “The peoples that you have removed and placed in the cities of Samaria do not know the requirements of the God of the land. Because of this, He has sent lions among them, which are indeed killing them off.” (17:26).
Then the king of Assyria commanded: “Send back one of the priests you carried off from Samaria, and have him go back to live there and teach the requirements of the God of the land.” (17:27).
Thus one of the priests they had carried away came and lived in Bethel, and he began to teach them how they should worship the LORD. (17:28).

Nevertheless, the people of each nation continued to make their own gods in the cities where they had settled, and they set them up in the shrines that the people of Samaria had made on the high places. (17:29).
The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth, the men of Cuth made Nergal, the men of Hamath made Ashima, (17:30).
the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech the gods of Sepharvaim. (17:31).
So the new residents worshiped the LORD, but they also appointed for themselves priests of all sorts to serve in the shrines of the high places. (17:32).
They worshiped the LORD, but they also served their own gods according to the customs of the nations from which they had been carried away. (17:33).

To this day they are still practicing their former customs. None of them worship the LORD or observe the statutes, ordinances, laws, and commandments that the LORD gave the descendants of Jacob, whom He named Israel. (17:34).
For the LORD had made a covenant with the Israelites and commanded them, “Do not worship other gods or bow down to them; do not serve them or sacrifice to them. (17:35).
Instead, worship the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm. You are to bow down to Him and offer sacrifices to Him. (17:36).
And you must always be careful to observe the statutes, ordinances, laws, and commandments He wrote for you. Do not worship other gods. (17:37).
Do not forget the covenant I have made with you. Do not worship other gods, (17:38).
but worship the LORD your God, and He will deliver you from the hands of all your enemies.” (17:39).
But they would not listen, and they persisted in their former customs. (17:40).
So these nations worshiped the LORD but also served their idols, and to this day their children and grandchildren continue to do as their fathers did. (17:41).
