translationNotes.note: Describes syncretism: outward reverence for YHWH combined with continued idolatry.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

Verse 6 carries Israel off to Halah, the Habor river, and the cities of the Medes, and verse 24 brings people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim into Samaria. This was deliberate Assyrian policy in both directions: move the leading families out, move strangers in, and no nation can regroup around its own land, language, and shrine. Sargon II's annals claim 27,000 taken from Samaria in 722 BC.

Verse 16 lists worship of the host of heaven alongside the calves and the Asherah. The phrase means the sun, moon, planets, and stars treated as powers to be served, the state religion of Assyria and Babylon. Deuteronomy 4:19 and 17:2-5 forbid it by name, and Josiah later has to clear out priests appointed for the sun, moon, and constellations (2 Kings 23:5).

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel’s exile is explained theologically: persistent idolatry and rejection of God’s covenant led to their removal. Assyria’s resettlement policy created a mixed population in Samaria, later known as the Samaritans.

headings.text: Hoshea the Last King of Israel

stories.title: 🛡️ 2 Kings 18
summaryBullets: In the third year of the reign of Hoshea son of Elah over Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz became king of Judah. (18:1).
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Abi, the daughter of Zechariah. (18:2).
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done. (18:3).

He removed the high places, shattered the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah poles. He also demolished the bronze snake called Nehushtan that Moses had made, for up to that time the Israelites had burned incense to it. (18:4).
Hezekiah trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. No king of Judah was like him, either before him or after him. (18:5).
He remained faithful to the LORD and did not turn from following Him; he kept the commandments that the LORD had given Moses. (18:6).
And the LORD was with Hezekiah, and he prospered wherever he went. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him. (18:7).
He defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza and its borders, from watchtower to fortified city. (18:8).
In the fourth year of Hezekiah’s reign, which was the seventh year of the reign of Hoshea son of Elah over Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria marched against Samaria and besieged it. (18:9).
And at the end of three years, the Assyrians captured it. So Samaria was captured in the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel. (18:10).
The king of Assyria exiled the Israelites to Assyria and settled them in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes. (18:11).

This happened because they did not listen to the voice of the LORD their God, but violated His covenant— all that Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded — and would neither listen nor obey. (18:12).
In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah. (18:13).

So Hezekiah king of Judah sent word to the king of Assyria at Lachish, saying, “I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand from me.” And the king of Assyria exacted from Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold. (18:14).
Hezekiah gave him all the silver that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace. (18:15).
At that time Hezekiah stripped the gold with which he had plated the doors and doorposts of the temple of the LORD, and he gave it to the king of Assyria. (18:16).

Nevertheless, the king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh, along with a great army, from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. They advanced up to Jerusalem and stationed themselves by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer’s Field. (18:17).
Then they called for the king. And Eliakim son of Hilkiah the palace administrator, Shebnah the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder, went out to them. (18:18).
The Rabshakeh said to them, “Tell Hezekiah that this is what the great king, the king of Assyria, says: What is the basis of this confidence of yours? (18:19).
You claim to have a strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words. In whom are you now trusting, that you have rebelled against me? (18:20).
Look now, you are trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. (18:21).

But if you say to me, ‘We trust in the LORD our God,’ is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem: ‘You must worship before this altar in Jerusalem’? (18:22).
Now, therefore, make a bargain with my master, the king of Assyria. I will give you two thousand horses — if you can put riders on them! (18:23).
For how can you repel a single officer among the least of my master’s servants when you depend on Egypt for chariots and horsemen? (18:24).
So now, was it apart from the LORD that I have come up against this place to destroy it? The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’” (18:25).

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, along with Shebnah and Joah, said to the Rabshakeh, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it. Do not speak with us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall.” (18:26).

But the Rabshakeh replied, “Has my master sent me to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are destined with you to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?” (18:27).
Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew: “Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria! (18:28).
This is what the king says: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you; he cannot deliver you from my hand. (18:29).
Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the LORD when he says, ‘The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.’ (18:30).

Do not listen to Hezekiah, for this is what the king of Assyria says: Make peace with me and come out to me. Then every one of you will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree and drink water from his own cistern, (18:31).

until I come and take you away to a land like your own— a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees and honey— so that you may live and not die. But do not listen to Hezekiah, for he misleads you when he says, ‘The LORD will deliver us.’ (18:32).
Has the god of any nation ever delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria? (18:33).
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand? (18:34).
Who among all the gods of these lands has delivered his land from my hand? How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?” (18:35).
But the people remained silent and did not answer a word, for Hezekiah had commanded, “Do not answer him.” (18:36).

Then Hilkiah’s son Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and Asaph’s son Joah the recorder came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and they relayed to him the words of the Rabshakeh. (18:37).

Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.

Verses 14 to 16 record Hezekiah paying three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, stripping the temple doors to raise it. Sennacherib had the campaign written up on clay prisms, copies of which are in London, Chicago, and Jerusalem. He never claims to have taken the city.

The officials ask the Rabshakeh in verse 26 to speak Aramaic, which they understood, and not Judean, the Hebrew of the street, in the hearing of the men on the wall. Aramaic was the diplomatic language of the whole region; ordinary people in Jerusalem did not yet know it. He raises his voice and keeps to Hebrew on purpose, because the speech is aimed at the defenders and not at their government.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hezekiah becomes king of Judah at twenty-five, removes idolatrous sites and objects, and successfully resists Assyria until Sennacherib attacks in his fourteenth year; after paying tribute, Hezekiah's officials hear the Assyrian field commander's taunting speech demanding Jerusalem's surrender.

stories.title: 🛡️ 2 Kings 19
summaryBullets: On hearing this report, King Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and entered the house of the LORD. (19:1).
And he sent Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and the leading priests, all wearing sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz (19:2).
to tell him, “This is what Hezekiah says: Today is a day of distress, rebuke, and disgrace; for children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them. (19:3).

Perhaps the LORD your God will hear all the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to defy the living God, and He will rebuke him for the words that the LORD your God has heard. Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives.” (19:4).
So the servants of King Hezekiah went to Isaiah, (19:5).
who replied, “Tell your master that this is what the LORD says: ‘Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed Me. (19:6).
Behold, I will put a spirit in him so that he will hear a rumor and return to his own land, where I will cause him to fall by the sword.’” (19:7).
When the Rabshakeh heard that the king of Assyria had left Lachish, he withdrew and found the king fighting against Libnah. (19:8).
Now Sennacherib had been warned about Tirhakah king of Cush: “Look, he has set out to fight against you.” So Sennacherib again sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying, (19:9).
“Give this message to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you by saying that Jerusalem will not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria. (19:10).
Surely you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the other countries, devoting them to destruction. Will you then be spared? (19:11).
Did the gods of the nations destroyed by my fathers rescue those nations— the gods of Gozan, Haran, and Rezeph, and of the people of Eden in Telassar? (19:12).
Where are the kings of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?’” (19:13).
So Hezekiah received the letter from the messengers, read it, and went up to the house of the LORD and spread it out before the LORD. (19:14).
And Hezekiah prayed before the LORD: “O LORD, God of Israel, enthroned between the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth. (19:15).
Incline Your ear, O LORD, and hear; open Your eyes, O LORD, and see. Listen to the words that Sennacherib has sent to defy the living God. (19:16).
Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste these nations and their lands. (19:17).
They have cast their gods into the fire and destroyed them, for they were not gods, but only wood and stone — the work of human hands. (19:18).
And now, O LORD our God, please save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God.” (19:19).
Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent a message to Hezekiah: “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I have heard your prayer concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria. (19:20).
This is the word that the LORD has spoken against him: ‘The Virgin Daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you; the Daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head behind you. (19:21).
Whom have you taunted and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes in pride? Against the Holy One of Israel! (19:22).

Through your servants you have taunted the Lord, and you have said: “With my many chariots I have ascended to the heights of the mountains, to the remote peaks of Lebanon. I have cut down its tallest cedars, the finest of its cypresses. I have reached its farthest outposts, the densest of its forests. (19:23).
I have dug wells and drunk foreign waters. With the soles of my feet I have dried up all the streams of Egypt.” (19:24).
Have you not heard? Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it. Now I have brought it to pass, that you should crush fortified cities into piles of rubble. (19:25).
Therefore their inhabitants, devoid of power, are dismayed and ashamed. They are like plants in the field, tender green shoots, grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown. (19:26).
But I know your sitting down, your going out and coming in, and your raging against Me. (19:27).
Because your rage and arrogance against Me have reached My ears, I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth; I will send you back the way you came.’ (19:28).

And this will be a sign to you, O Hezekiah: This year you will eat what grows on its own, and in the second year what springs from the same. But in the third year you will sow and reap; you will plant vineyards and eat their fruit. (19:29).
And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah will again take root below and bear fruit above. (19:30).
For a remnant will go forth from Jerusalem, and survivors from Mount Zion. The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this. (19:31).
So this is what the LORD says about the king of Assyria: ‘He will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it. He will not come before it with a shield or build up a siege ramp against it. (19:32).
He will go back the way he came, and he will not enter this city, declares the LORD. (19:33).
I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.’” (19:34).
And that very night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians. When the people got up the next morning, there were all the dead bodies! (19:35).
So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and withdrew. He returned to Nineveh and stayed there. (19:36).

One day, while he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer put him to the sword and escaped to the land of Ararat. And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place. (19:37).
crossRefs: Isaiah 37:1-38: The same prayer, the same word from Isaiah, and the same night in the Assyrian camp.
2 Chronicles 32:20-23: The parallel account, where the LORD sends an angel who cuts off the commanders and officers in the camp.
Psalm 46:1-11: God is a very present help in trouble; He makes wars cease and says be still and know that I am God.
Isaiah 10:5-19: Assyria is the rod of God's anger, but the axe does not boast over the one who swings it.
Ezra 4:2: Esarhaddon king of Assyria, the son named in verse 37, settles foreign peoples in the land.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְחֻשְׁתָּן (Nehushtan), Greek: Νεεσθάν (Nee-than), Aramaic: נחשׁתן (Nehushtan)
translationNotes.note: Name mocking the bronze serpent: means 'a mere piece of bronze.' Hezekiah destroys it because it became an object of idolatry.
Not a personal name, but a military title meaning 'chief officer/cupbearer.'

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה (mal’akh YHWH), Greek: ἄγγελος Κυρίου (angelos Kyriou), Aramaic: מלאכא דיהוה (malaka d’YHWH)
translationNotes.note: Messenger of YHWH; often appears with divine authority, sometimes indistinguishable from God’s own presence.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲלוֹת אָחָז (ma‘alot Ahaz), Greek: ἀναβαθμοί (anabathmoi), Aramaic: מעלות אחז (ma‘lot Ahaz)
translationNotes.note: A stepped structure used to measure the sun’s shadow. The backward movement signified God’s miraculous confirmation.

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.

Verse 35 reports the Assyrian army struck in one night and Sennacherib withdrawing to Nineveh without taking Jerusalem. Herodotus, writing about 440 BC, records an Egyptian account of the same campaign in which Sennacherib's army was disabled overnight at Pelusium and had to retreat (Histories 2.141). His own annals never claim the city. Verse 37 has him murdered by two of his sons, which Babylonian chronicle tablets date to 681 BC.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hezekiah tears his clothes and sends officials to Isaiah, who promises the Lord will turn Sennacherib away; Sennacherib sends another message mocking Jerusalem's God, but Isaiah declares the city will be spared. That night the angel of the Lord kills 185,000 Assyrian soldiers, and Sennacherib withdraws to Nineveh where his own sons later assassinate him.

stories.title: 🛡️ 2 Kings 20
summaryBullets: In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.’” (20:1).
Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD, saying, (20:2).
“Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what is good in Your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly. (20:3).
Before Isaiah had left the middle courtyard, the word of the LORD came to him, saying, (20:4).

“Go back and tell Hezekiah the leader of My people that this is what the LORD, the God of your father David, says: ‘I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. I will surely heal you. On the third day from now you will go up to the house of the LORD. (20:5).
I will add fifteen years to your life. And I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria. I will defend this city for My sake and for the sake of My servant David.’” (20:6).
Then Isaiah said, “Prepare a poultice of figs.” So they brought it and applied it to the boil, and Hezekiah recovered. (20:7).
Now Hezekiah had asked Isaiah, “What will be the sign that the LORD will heal me and that I will go up to the house of the LORD on the third day?” (20:8).
And Isaiah had replied, “This will be a sign to you from the LORD that He will do what He has promised: Would you like the shadow to go forward ten steps, or back ten steps?” (20:9).
“It is easy for the shadow to lengthen ten steps,” answered Hezekiah, “but not for it to go back ten steps.” (20:10).
So Isaiah the prophet called out to the LORD, and He brought the shadow back the ten steps it had descended on the stairway of Ahaz. (20:11).
At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard about Hezekiah’s illness. (20:12).

And Hezekiah received the envoys and showed them all that was in his treasure house — the silver, the gold, the spices, and the precious oil, as well as his armory— all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them. (20:13).
Then the prophet Isaiah went to King Hezekiah and asked, “Where did those men come from, and what did they say to you?” “They came from a distant land,” Hezekiah replied, “from Babylon.” (20:14).
“What have they seen in your palace?” Isaiah asked. “They have seen everything in my palace,” answered Hezekiah. “There is nothing among my treasures that I did not show them.” (20:15).
Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD: (20:16).
The time will surely come when everything in your palace and all that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD. (20:17).
And some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” (20:18).
But Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.” For he thought, “Will there not at least be peace and security in my lifetime?” (20:19).

As for the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, along with all his might and how he constructed the pool and the tunnel to bring water into the city, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (20:20).
And Hezekiah rested with his fathers, and his son Manasseh reigned in his place. (20:21).
crossRefs: Isaiah 38:1-22: The same illness, the same fifteen years, and Hezekiah's written prayer after he recovered.
Isaiah 39:1-8: The same envoys from Merodach-baladan and the same word that all of it will be carried to Babylon.
2 Chronicles 32:24-31: The parallel account, adding that God left him to himself to test what was in his heart.
Joshua 10:12-14: The sun stands still over Gibeon and the moon over the Valley of Aijalon for about a whole day.
2 Kings 24:10-16: Babylon carries off the treasures of the house of the LORD and the leading men, exactly as Isaiah said.

Not a personal name, but a military title meaning 'chief officer/cupbearer.'

translationNotes.note: A stepped structure used to measure the sun’s shadow. The backward movement signified God’s miraculous confirmation.

Isaiah calls for a pressed lump of dried figs to be laid on the boil (verse 7). Figs were sold and stored as compressed cakes, and a poultice of them was an ordinary treatment for a swelling. The sign Hezekiah is given is the shadow on the steps, not the figs; the figs are common medicine applied alongside it.

A Chaldean chief who twice seized the throne of Babylon and spent his life resisting Assyria, ruling from 721 to 710 BC and again briefly in 703. Assyrian records name him repeatedly as Marduk-apla-iddina II. An envoy sent from him to Jerusalem was not a courtesy call about an illness; he was recruiting allies for a revolt against the same empire that had just swallowed Samaria.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hezekiah recovers from a fatal illness after Isaiah promises healing and God makes a shadow move backward ten steps as a sign; later, when envoys from Babylon visit and Hezekiah shows them his treasures, Isaiah warns that everything will be carried to Babylon and some of his descendants will be taken as eunuchs.

stories.title: ⚠️ 2 Kings 21
summaryBullets: Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem fifty-five years. His mother’s name was Hephzibah. (21:1).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD by following the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites. (21:2).

For he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had destroyed, and he raised up altars for Baal. He made an Asherah pole, as King Ahab of Israel had done, and he worshiped and served all the host of heaven. (21:3).
Manasseh also built altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, “In Jerusalem I will put My Name.” (21:4).
In both courtyards of the house of the LORD, he built altars to all the host of heaven. (21:5).
He sacrificed his own son in the fire, practiced sorcery and divination, and consulted mediums and spiritists. He did great evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger. (21:6).

Manasseh even took the carved Asherah pole he had made and set it up in the temple, of which the LORD had said to David and his son Solomon, “In this temple and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will establish My Name forever. (21:7).

I will never again cause the feet of the Israelites to wander from the land that I gave to their fathers, if only they are careful to do all I have commanded them— the whole Law that My servant Moses commanded them.” (21:8).
But the people did not listen and Manasseh led them astray, so that they did greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites. (21:9).
And the LORD spoke through His servants the prophets, saying, (21:10).
“Since Manasseh king of Judah has committed all these abominations, acting more wickedly than the Amorites who preceded him, and with his idols has caused Judah to sin, (21:11).
this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Behold, I am bringing such calamity upon Jerusalem and Judah that the news will reverberate in the ears of all who hear it. (21:12).

I will stretch out over Jerusalem the measuring line used against Samaria and the plumb line used against the house of Ahab, and I will wipe out Jerusalem as one wipes out a bowl— wiping it and turning it upside down. (21:13).
So I will forsake the remnant of My inheritance and deliver them into the hands of their enemies. And they will become plunder and spoil to all their enemies, (21:14).
because they have done evil in My sight and have provoked Me to anger from the day their fathers came out of Egypt until this day.’” (21:15).
Moreover, Manasseh shed so much innocent blood that he filled Jerusalem from end to end, in addition to the sin that he had caused Judah to commit, doing evil in the sight of the LORD. (21:16).
As for the rest of the acts of Manasseh, along with all his accomplishments and the sin that he committed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (21:17).
And Manasseh rested with his fathers and was buried in his palace garden, the garden of Uzza. And his son Amon reigned in his place. (21:18).
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem two years. His mother’s name was Meshullemeth daughter of Haruz; she was from Jotbah. (21:19).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh had done. (21:20).
He walked in all the ways of his father, and he served and worshiped the idols his father had served. (21:21).
He abandoned the LORD, the God of his fathers, and did not walk in the way of the LORD. (21:22).
Then the servants of Amon conspired against him and killed the king in his palace. (21:23).
But the people of the land killed all those who had conspired against King Amon, and they made his son Josiah king in his place. (21:24).
As for the rest of the acts of Amon, along with his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (21:25).
And he was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah reigned in his place. (21:26).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 18:9-14: Do not imitate the detestable practices of the nations: passing a child through fire, divination, omens, sorcery, mediums, and necromancers.
Leviticus 20:1-5: Whoever gives any of his children to Molech is to be put to death, and God will set His face against him and his family.
2 Chronicles 33:1-20: The parallel account, with Manasseh taken to Babylon with hooks, his prayer, and his return.
2 Kings 23:26-27: The LORD did not turn from His burning anger, because of all the provocations of Manasseh.
Jeremiah 15:4: I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of Manasseh son of Hezekiah.

translationNotes.note: A Canaanite goddess, and also the carved wooden pole or tree that stood for her beside an altar. Verse 3 has Manasseh make one, and verse 7 has him set the carved image inside the temple itself. Deuteronomy 16:21 forbids planting one beside the altar of the LORD by name, and inscriptions found at Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai show Israelites pairing her name with the LORD's, which is the exact mixture the reforming kings tear out.

Verse 5 has Manasseh build altars for all the host of heaven in both courts of the temple, and verse 7 puts a carved Asherah image inside the house itself. The offence recorded is not that he worshipped elsewhere but that he installed the astral cult and the goddess inside the building God had named as His own, on the site verse 4 says God had claimed by name.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוֹב (ov), medium - יִדְּעֹנִי (yiddeoni), spiritist - כֶּשֶׁף (keshef), sorcery
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 lists what Manasseh practised: burning his own son in the fire, sorcery, reading omens, and consulting mediums and spiritists. That is not a loose description. Deuteronomy 18:10-12 forbids the same catalogue item by item, beginning with anyone who makes his son or daughter pass through the fire and running through divination, augury, sorcery, charming, mediums, spiritists, and consulting the dead, and calls each of them an abomination.

translationNotes.term: The measuring line and the plumb line
translationNotes.note: Verse 13 turns two builder's tools around. A cord marks out where walls go and a weighted string checks that they stand true, and the sentence has both applied to Jerusalem the way they were applied to Samaria and the house of Ahab, to mark out demolition rather than construction. Amos 7:7-8 uses the plumb line the same way. The verse then adds the picture of a dish wiped clean and turned upside down.

Verse 1 gives Manasseh the longest reign of any king of Israel or Judah, fifty-five years, longer than David or Solomon. The parallel account adds an episode Kings does not carry: 2 Chronicles 33:11-13 records Assyrian commanders taking him with hooks, binding him in bronze fetters, carrying him to Babylon, and God restoring him to Jerusalem after he humbled himself. Both accounts stand as written.

stories.keyTakeaway: Manasseh becomes king at twelve and spends fifty-five years promoting idol worship, sacrificing his own son, and shedding innocent blood; God declares through prophets that Jerusalem will be destroyed as punishment. After Manasseh's death, his son Amon reigns briefly, continues his father's evil practices, is assassinated by his officials, and is succeeded by his son Josiah.

stories.title: ⚠️ 2 Kings 22
summaryBullets: Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem thirty-one years. His mother’s name was Jedidah daughter of Adaiah; she was from Bozkath. (22:1).
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in all the ways of his father David; he did not turn aside to the right or to the left. (22:2).
Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, King Josiah sent the scribe, Shaphan son of Azaliah, the son of Meshullam, to the house of the LORD, saying, (22:3).
“Go up to Hilkiah the high priest and have him count the money that has been brought into the house of the LORD, which the doorkeepers have collected from the people. (22:4).

And let them deliver it into the hands of the supervisors of those doing the work on the house of the LORD, who in turn are to give it to the workmen repairing the damages to the house of the LORD — (22:5).
to the carpenters, builders, and masons — to buy timber and dressed stone to repair the temple. (22:6).
But they need not account for the money put into their hands, since they work with integrity.” (22:7).
Then Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD!” And he gave it to Shaphan, who read it. (22:8).

And Shaphan the scribe went to the king and reported, “Your servants have paid out the money that was found in the temple and have put it into the hands of the workers and supervisors of the house of the LORD.” (22:9).
Moreover , Shaphan the scribe told the king, “Hilkiah the priest has given me a book.” And Shaphan read it in the presence of the king. (22:10).
When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes (22:11).
and commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the servant of the king: (22:12).

“Go and inquire of the LORD for me, for the people, and for all Judah concerning the words in this book that has been found. For great is the wrath of the LORD that burns against us because our fathers have not obeyed the words of this book by doing all that is written about us.” (22:13).

So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went and spoke to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, the keeper of the wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem, in the Second District. (22:14).
And Huldah said to them, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Tell the man who sent you (22:15).
that this is what the LORD says: I am about to bring calamity on this place and on its people, according to all the words of the book that the king of Judah has read, (22:16).

because they have forsaken Me and burned incense to other gods, that they might provoke Me to anger with all the works of their hands. My wrath will be kindled against this place and will not be quenched.’ (22:17).
But as for the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, tell him that this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘As for the words that you heard, (22:18).

because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before the LORD when you heard what I spoke against this place and against its people, that they would become a desolation and a curse, and because you have torn your clothes and wept before Me, I have heard you,’ declares the LORD. (22:19).

‘Therefore I will indeed gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see all the calamity that I will bring on this place.’” So they brought her answer back to the king. (22:20).
crossRefs: 2 Chronicles 34:1-33: The parallel account, in which Josiah's purge of the high places begins before the book is found.
Deuteronomy 31:24-26: Moses writes the words of this law in a book and has it placed beside the ark as a witness against Israel.
Deuteronomy 28:15-68: The curses read out for breaking the covenant, the words that make Josiah tear his clothes.
Deuteronomy 17:18-20: The king is to write himself a copy of this law in the presence of the Levitical priests and read it all his life.
Nehemiah 8:1-9: Ezra reads the law before the assembly from early morning until midday, and the people weep as they hear it.

translationNotes.note: A book at this period is a scroll of leather or papyrus sheets sewn end to end and rolled, not a bound volume. The sanctuary was where such a document belonged: Moses commanded the book of the law be put beside the ark as a witness (Deuteronomy 31:24-26), and Joshua wrote in the book of the law of God and set a stone up at the sanctuary (Joshua 24:26). Finding one in the temple is unremarkable; the state of a kingdom that had lost track of it is not.

The garment was torn from the neck downward and left unmended, so the sign stayed visible for days. It marked news of a death (Genesis 37:34), defeat, and blasphemy heard by a court (Matthew 26:65), and Hezekiah's officials come to him with their clothes torn after hearing the Assyrian envoy (2 Kings 18:37). The high priest alone was forbidden to do it (Leviticus 21:10). Verse 19 has God name the act itself as part of the reason for the answer given.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּרַשׁ (darash), to seek or enquire
translationNotes.note: Verse 13 is a formal procedure, not a private prayer. A king facing a decision sent named officials to a recognised prophet and received an answer to bring back; Jehoshaphat demands it before a campaign (1 Kings 22:5-8), and 1 Samuel 9:9 explains that going to enquire of God meant going to the man called a seer. Here the delegation is the high priest and four senior officers of state.

Verse 14 places Huldah in the mishneh of Jerusalem, a named quarter of the city rather than a vague neighbourhood. It was the newer district on the western hill, outside the old City of David, and Zephaniah 1:10 names it in the same period as a place where the sound of wailing would be heard. The delegation walks across the city to a specific address.

The royal secretary of this chapter heads a family that keeps appearing for the next forty years. His son Ahikam protects Jeremiah from a mob calling for his death (Jeremiah 26:24), his son Gemariah owns the room the scroll is read from (Jeremiah 36:10), and his grandson Gedaliah is made governor of Judah after Jerusalem falls (2 Kings 25:22). A clay seal impression reading 'belonging to Gemaryahu son of Shaphan' was excavated in the City of David.

stories.keyTakeaway: Josiah discovers the Book of the Law during temple repairs; he tears his robes in distress and sends officials to consult the prophet Huldah, who warns of coming disaster on Judah but promises Josiah himself will die in peace before it arrives.

headings.text: Hilkiah Finds the Book of the Law

stories.title: ⚠️ 2 Kings 23
summaryBullets: Then the king summoned all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. (23:1).

And he went up to the house of the LORD with all the people of Judah and Jerusalem, as well as the priests and the prophets— all the people small and great— and in their hearing he read all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD. (23:2).

So the king stood by the pillar and made a covenant before the LORD to follow the LORD and to keep His commandments, decrees, and statutes with all his heart and all his soul, and to carry out the words of the covenant that were written in this book. And all the people entered into the covenant. (23:3).

Then the king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, the priests second in rank, and the doorkeepers to remove from the temple of the LORD all the articles made for Baal, Asherah, and all the host of heaven. And he burned them outside Jerusalem in the fields of Kidron and carried their ashes to Bethel. (23:4).

Josiah also did away with the idolatrous priests ordained by the kings of Judah to burn incense on the high places of the cities of Judah and in the places all around Jerusalem — those who had burned incense to Baal, to the sun and moon, to the constellations, and to all the host of heaven. (23:5).

He brought the Asherah pole from the house of the LORD to the Kidron Valley outside Jerusalem, and there he burned it, ground it to powder, and threw its dust on the graves of the common people. (23:6).
He also tore down the quarters of the male shrine prostitutes that were in the house of the LORD, where the women had woven tapestries for Asherah. (23:7).

Then Josiah brought all the priests from the cities of Judah and desecrated the high places, from Geba to Beersheba, where the priests had burned incense. He tore down the high places of the gates at the entrance of the gate of Joshua the governor of the city, which was to the left of the city gate. (23:8).
Although the priests of the high places did not come up to the altar of the LORD in Jerusalem, they ate unleavened bread with their fellow priests. (23:9).
He also desecrated Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech. (23:10).

And he removed from the entrance to the house of the LORD the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun. They were in the court near the chamber of an official named Nathan-melech. And Josiah burned up the chariots of the sun. (23:11).

He pulled down the altars that the kings of Judah had set up on the roof near the upper chamber of Ahaz, and the altars that Manasseh had set up in the two courtyards of the house of the LORD. The king pulverized them there and threw their dust into the Kidron Valley. (23:12).

The king also desecrated the high places east of Jerusalem, to the south of the Mount of Corruption, which King Solomon of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Sidonians, for Chemosh the abomination of the Moabites, and for Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. (23:13).
He smashed the sacred pillars to pieces, cut down the Asherah poles, and covered the sites with human bones. (23:14).

He even pulled down the altar at Bethel, the high place set up by Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had caused Israel to sin. Then he burned the high place, ground it to powder, and burned the Asherah pole. (23:15).

And as Josiah turned, he saw the tombs there on the hillside, and he sent someone to take the bones out of the tombs, and he burned them on the altar to defile it, according to the word of the LORD proclaimed by the man of God who had foretold these things. (23:16).

Then the king asked, “What is this monument I see?” And the men of the city replied, “It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and proclaimed these things that you have done to the altar of Bethel.” (23:17).
“Let him rest,” said Josiah. “Do not let anyone disturb his bones.” So they left his bones undisturbed, along with those of the prophet who had come from Samaria. (23:18).
Just as Josiah had done at Bethel, so also in the cities of Samaria he removed all the shrines of the high places set up by the kings of Israel who had provoked the LORD to anger. (23:19).
On the altars he slaughtered all the priests of the high places, and he burned human bones on them. Then he returned to Jerusalem. (23:20).
The king commanded all the people, “Keep the Passover of the LORD your God, as it is written in this Book of the Covenant.” (23:21).
No such Passover had been observed from the days of the judges who had governed Israel through all the days of the kings of Israel and Judah. (23:22).
But in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign, this Passover was observed to the LORD in Jerusalem. (23:23).

Furthermore, Josiah removed the mediums and spiritists, the household gods and idols, and all the abominations that were seen in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem. He did this to carry out the words of the law written in the book that Hilkiah the priest had found in the house of the LORD. (23:24).
Neither before nor after Josiah was there any king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his strength, according to all the Law of Moses. (23:25).
Nevertheless, the LORD did not turn away from the fury of His burning anger, which was kindled against Judah because of all that Manasseh had done to provoke Him to anger. (23:26).

For the LORD had said, “I will remove Judah from My sight, just as I removed Israel. I will reject this city Jerusalem, which I chose, and the temple of which I said, ‘My Name shall be there.’” (23:27).
As for the rest of the acts of Josiah and all his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (23:28).

During Josiah’s reign, Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt marched up to help the king of Assyria at the Euphrates River. King Josiah went out to confront him, but Neco faced him and killed him at Megiddo. (23:29).

From Megiddo his servants carried his body in a chariot, brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own tomb. Then the people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in place of his father. (23:30).
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months. His mother’s name was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah; she was from Libnah. (23:31).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his fathers had done. (23:32).

And Pharaoh Neco imprisoned Jehoahaz at Riblah in the land of Hamath so that he could not reign in Jerusalem, and he imposed on Judah a levy of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. (23:33).

Then Pharaoh Neco made Eliakim son of Josiah king in place of his father Josiah, and he changed Eliakim’s name to Jehoiakim. But Neco took Jehoahaz and carried him off to Egypt, where he died. (23:34).
So Jehoiakim paid the silver and gold to Pharaoh Neco, but to meet Pharaoh’s demand he taxed the land and exacted the silver and the gold from the people, each according to his wealth. (23:35).
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eleven years. His mother’s name was Zebidah daughter of Pedaiah; she was from Rumah. (23:36).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his fathers had done. (23:37).

The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

About 75 lbs (34 kg) of metal. A 'talent of gold' in the Old Testament (e.g. 2 Samuel 12:30) refers to physical mass rather than coined currency. The bronze for the Tabernacle (Exodus 38:29) was 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

translationNotes.term: Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom
translationNotes.note: Verse 10 has Josiah defile the Topheth so that no one could make a son or daughter pass through fire to Molech. The Valley of Hinnom runs along the south and west of Jerusalem, and the Topheth was the burning ground inside it where children were put into the fire before the image of Molech, the god of Ammon. Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2-5 set death as the penalty, and Jeremiah 7:31 and 32:35 say God never commanded it and it never entered His mind. The Greek form of the valley's name, Gehenna, is the word Jesus uses for hell (Mark 9:43-48).

Verse 11 removes horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun, stabled at the entrance of the temple, and burns the chariots of the sun. Sun worship across Assyria and Syria pictured the sun crossing the sky in a chariot, and real horses and chariots were kept and paraded for it. They had been standing at the door of the house of the LORD.

Verse 7 tears down the quarters of the qedeshim inside the temple precinct, where women were weaving hangings for the Asherah. The word means ones set apart, and it names men attached to a shrine whose service to the fertility cult was sexual. Deuteronomy 23:17-18 bans the practice in both the male and female form and refuses their earnings at the sanctuary.

stories.keyTakeaway: King Josiah reads the Book of the Covenant to all Judah and Jerusalem, renews the covenant with the LORD, and systematically destroys idols and pagan altars throughout the land; he celebrates Passover and then dies in battle against Pharaoh Necho, after which his son Jehoahaz reigns briefly before being deposed by Egypt in favor of another son, Jehoiakim.

stories.title: 🔥 2 Kings 24
summaryBullets: During Jehoiakim’s reign, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon invaded. So Jehoiakim became his vassal for three years, until he turned and rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar. (24:1).

And the LORD sent Chaldean, Aramean, Moabite, and Ammonite raiders against Jehoiakim in order to destroy Judah, according to the word that the LORD had spoken through His servants the prophets. (24:2).
Surely this happened to Judah at the LORD’s command, to remove them from His presence because of the sins of Manasseh and all that he had done, (24:3).
and also for the innocent blood he had shed. For he had filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD was unwilling to forgive. (24:4).
As for the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, along with all his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (24:5).
And Jehoiakim rested with his fathers, and his son Jehoiachin reigned in his place. (24:6).
Now the king of Egypt did not march out of his land again, because the king of Babylon had taken all his territory, from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River. (24:7).
Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months. His mother’s name was Nehushta daughter of Elnathan; she was from Jerusalem. (24:8).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his father had done. (24:9).
At that time the servants of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched up to Jerusalem, and the city came under siege. (24:10).
And Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to the city while his servants were besieging it. (24:11).

Jehoiachin king of Judah, his mother, his servants, his commanders, and his officials all surrendered to the king of Babylon. So in the eighth year of his reign, the king of Babylon took him captive. (24:12).

As the LORD had declared, Nebuchadnezzar also carried off all the treasures from the house of the LORD and the royal palace, and he cut into pieces all the gold articles that Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the LORD. (24:13).

He carried into exile all Jerusalem — all the commanders and mighty men of valor, all the craftsmen and metalsmiths — ten thousand captives in all. Only the poorest people of the land remained. (24:14).
Nebuchadnezzar carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon, as well as the king’s mother, his wives, his officials, and the leading men of the land. He took them into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon. (24:15).
The king of Babylon also brought into exile to Babylon all seven thousand men of valor and a thousand craftsmen and metalsmiths— all strong and fit for battle. (24:16).
Then the king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s uncle, king in his place and changed his name to Zedekiah. (24:17).
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eleven years. His mother’s name was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah; she was from Libnah. (24:18).
And Zedekiah did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as Jehoiakim had done. (24:19).
For because of the anger of the LORD, all this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until He finally banished them from His presence. And Zedekiah also rebelled against the king of Babylon. (24:20).

translationNotes.note: Babylonian king who showed favor to Jehoiachin. His name means 'Man of Marduk.'

Ten thousand; also used idiomatically for 'countless.' Revelation 5:11's 'ten thousands of ten thousands' (myriades myriadon) of angels could be 100 million as a literal floor, though the intent is more naturally read as 'innumerable.'

Verses 14 and 16 single out a thousand craftsmen and metalworkers among the ten thousand deported in 597 BC. This was policy, not chance: without smiths a subject nation cannot make weapons, repair armour, or fortify, and the skills go to work for the empire instead. The Philistines had used the same method on Israel centuries earlier (1 Samuel 13:19-22).

Verse 15 carries the young king off to Babylon, and 2 Kings 25:27-30 has him released from prison thirty-seven years later and eating at the king's table. Administrative tablets excavated in Babylon list rations of oil issued to Yaukin, king of the land of Yahud, and to his sons, which is the same man under his fuller name Jehoiachin.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, takes Jehoiachin prisoner after a three-month reign, strips the temple of its treasures, and exiles ten thousand people to Babylon; he then installs Zedekiah as a puppet king.

stories.title: 🔥 2 Kings 25
summaryBullets: So in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his entire army. They encamped outside the city and built a siege wall all around it. (25:1).
And the city was kept under siege until King Zedekiah’s eleventh year. (25:2).
By the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine in the city was so severe that the people of the land had no food. (25:3).

Then the city was breached; and though the Chaldeans had surrounded the city, all the men of war fled by night by way of the gate between the two walls near the king’s garden. They headed toward the Arabah, (25:4).
but the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook him in the plains of Jericho, and his whole army deserted him. (25:5).
The Chaldeans seized the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where they pronounced judgment on him. (25:6).
And they slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes. Then they put out his eyes, bound him with bronze shackles, and took him to Babylon. (25:7).
On the seventh day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign over Babylon, Nebuzaradan captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, entered Jerusalem. (25:8).
He burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem — every significant building. (25:9).
And the whole army of the Chaldeans under the captain of the guard broke down the walls around Jerusalem. (25:10).
Then Nebuzaradan captain of the guard carried into exile the people who remained in the city, along with the deserters who had defected to the king of Babylon and the rest of the population. (25:11).
But the captain of the guard left behind some of the poorest of the land to tend the vineyards and fields. (25:12).
Moreover, the Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars and stands and the bronze Sea in the house of the LORD, and they carried the bronze to Babylon. (25:13).
They also took away the pots, shovels, wick trimmers, dishes, and all the articles of bronze used in the temple service. (25:14).
The captain of the guard also took away the censers and sprinkling bowls— anything made of pure gold or fine silver. (25:15).
As for the two pillars, the Sea, and the movable stands that Solomon had made for the house of the LORD, the weight of the bronze from all these articles was beyond measure. (25:16).

Each pillar was eighteen cubits tall. The bronze capital atop one pillar was three cubits high, with a network of bronze pomegranates all around. The second pillar, with its network, was similar. (25:17).
The captain of the guard also took away Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest of second rank, and the three doorkeepers. (25:18).

Of those still in the city, he took a court official who had been appointed over the men of war, as well as five royal advisors. He also took the scribe of the captain of the army, who had enlisted the people of the land, and sixty men who were found in the city. (25:19).
Nebuzaradan captain of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. (25:20).
There at Riblah in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death. So Judah was taken into exile, away from its own land. (25:21).
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, over the people he had left behind in the land of Judah. (25:22).

When all the commanders of the armies and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah as governor, they came to Gedaliah at Mizpah — Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah son of the Maacathite, as well as their men. (25:23).

And Gedaliah took an oath before them and their men, assuring them, “Do not be afraid of the servants of the Chaldeans. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you.” (25:24).

In the seventh month, however, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, who was a member of the royal family, came with ten men and struck down and killed Gedaliah, along with the Judeans and Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah. (25:25).
Then all the people small and great, together with the commanders of the army, arose and fled to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans. (25:26).

On the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Judah’s King Jehoiachin, in the year Evil-merodach became king of Babylon, he released King Jehoiachin of Judah from prison. (25:27).
And he spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and set his throne above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon. (25:28).
So Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes, and he dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life. (25:29).
And the king provided Jehoiachin a daily portion for the rest of his life. (25:30).

Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.

A town on the Orontes river in the land of Hamath, about two hundred miles north of Jerusalem, used as a forward headquarters by both empires: Pharaoh Neco held Jehoahaz there (2 Kings 23:33) and Nebuchadnezzar tries Zedekiah there in verse 6. Blinding a rebel vassal after making him watch his heirs die was standard Babylonian and Assyrian practice, meant to end the dynasty and leave a living warning.

Verse 8 dates the burning of the temple to the seventh day of the fifth month in Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year, which is 586 BC; Jeremiah 52:12 gives the tenth day. Seventy years later the exiles were still keeping a fast in the fifth month for it, which is the question put to Zechariah in Zechariah 7:3-5.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nebuchadnezzar's army besieges Jerusalem for over a year, breaks through the walls, captures Zedekiah, executes his sons before his eyes, and blinds him; Nebuzaradan burns the temple and city, demolishes the walls, carries off bronze temple furnishings and gold articles, executes priests and officials, and leaves the poor to tend vineyards under the appointed governor Gedaliah. Ishmael assassinates Gedaliah months later, prompting the remaining population to flee to Egypt; decades later, Jehoiachin is released from prison and given favor by the new Babylonian king.

intro:
2 Kings does not name its author. Jewish tradition (preserved in the Talmud, Baba Bathra 15a) attributes the book to the prophet Jeremiah, who drew on official court records and earlier prophetic histories. As with 1 Kings, the book cites "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel" and "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah" as its written sources. The book reached its final form during the Babylonian exile, around 560-550 BC, with the closing verses (2 Kings 25:27-30) recording the release of King Jehoiachin from Babylonian prison in 561 BC. Jeremiah was born around 645 BC in the priestly village of Anathoth, three miles north of Jerusalem, the son of Hilkiah the priest of the line of Abiathar. He was called to prophesy in 627 BC during the thirteenth year of King Josiah's reign, ministered through the reigns of five Judahite kings, and witnessed the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar II in 586 BC. Tradition holds that Jeremiah was taken against his will to Egypt by a remnant of Judahites after the fall and died there. The events of 2 Kings cover roughly 853 to 561 BC, spanning the closing decades of both kingdoms and the early years of the Babylonian exile. The historical setting runs from Iron Age IIB through the start of the exilic period, with the rise of the Neo-Assyrian Empire under Tiglath-Pileser III, Shalmaneser V, Sargon II, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon, and Ashurbanipal pressing first against Israel and then Judah. The northern kingdom of Israel fell to Assyria in 722 BC when Shalmaneser V and Sargon II captured Samaria and deported the ten northern tribes. In 701 BC Sennacherib invaded Judah and besieged Jerusalem during Hezekiah's reign. Assyria collapsed in the late seventh century; Nineveh fell to a Babylonian-Median coalition in 612 BC, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar II rose to dominance. Three Babylonian deportations of Judah followed: 605 BC (Daniel and other young nobles), 597 BC (King Jehoiachin and Ezekiel), and 586 BC (the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple). Egypt under the 26th Dynasty (Saite Period) and its Pharaoh Necho II remained a faltering counterweight to Babylonian power until his defeat at Carchemish in 605 BC.

2 Kings and 1 Kings were originally a single Hebrew book called Melakhim ("Kings"), divided by the Greek Septuagint translators (3rd century BC) and grouped with Samuel as "1-4 Kingdoms" (or "Reigns"); the Latin Vulgate inherited the division with the names "1-2 Kings" (following Samuel), and English Bibles followed this arrangement. In the Jewish canon, Kings is the fourth book of the Former Prophets (Nevi'im Rishonim). Hebrew manuscript fragments of Kings were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the 2nd and 1st centuries BC.
